articles.title: Is Nvidia's Legal Trouble Over - Or Just Beginning?
articles.body:
Is Nvidia's Legal Trouble Over - Or Just Beginning? (nypost.com) 64
			
		 	
				America's Justice Department "is still investigating Nvidia," reports the New York Post, adding that Monday President Trump posted on Truth Social that Nvidia should also "continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security."
But President Trump also told The New York Post Monday in an exclusive interview "that he's willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should 'tell the truth' to Congress when he testifies next week...
Huang doesn't need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added...  
The president said that Nvidia's success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he's even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year.  "I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late," Trump said. 
Earlier a source familiar with Jensen Huang's comeback "told the New York Post that President Trump and Vice President Vance 'became convinced that Jensen was a singular figure protecting Open Source models and preventing the closed-source model companies from becoming too powerful.'"
And CBS News reports that Nvidia's Jensen Huang "still has security clearance, sources say."  (Although revoking Huang's clearance "was discussed..."
It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances... [U.S. Attorney General Todd] Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information.
An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance.
Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime. "To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this ... that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said. Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings.
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
  
Jensen Huang is still testifying before the U.S. Congress next week, reports The Hill:
The Republican chairs of three different House committees stressed the need to address concerns regarding national security despite Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO..   "The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) wrote in a joint statement obtained by NewsNation... 
"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary's AI capabilities," it continued.
 
U.S. Senators are also promising to grill Nvidia's Jensen Huang, reports Politico, and to pass new legislation regulating future chip exports:
"The controversy with Nvidia ... is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," Senate Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton posted Monday.  "Congress has much to investigate," he said, "and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other." Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is also expected to testify Dec. 2, and one House Democratic aide said lawmakers are already "considering" asking other Nvidia board members to provide information....
Sen. Kevin Cramer, a member of Senate Banking, predicted that between Democrats outraged by Trump's backing of Huang and GOP wariness toward China, an export control measure would pass by a margin large enough "to overcome a veto."  Even if Huang ends up not participating in the hearings, or if Republicans back away under pressure from Trump, Democrats like incoming Banking Chair Elizabeth Warren could turbocharge their investigation plans using their new subpoena powers next year.  "Chairman Elizabeth Warren and a number of Banking Committee Republicans ... are going to put the screws to these people like they've never had the screws put to them before," Cramer said in an interview. 
Jensen Huang's scandal revealed that American export-control policy "remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy," according to Foreign Affairs (the magazine published by the nonprofit Council on Foreign Relations think tank). 
While the magazine applauded a recent tightening of restrictions, it suggests more action from Congress since the current administration's "lax enforcement of past controls — and internal divisions over the new ones — raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through."
As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track "on-chip" technologies — basically, features that can verify a chip's location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world's legacy chips.   Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. 
Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. [Another suggestion the article makes?  "[C]ondition advanced chip sales on the buyer's ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules."]  Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive...  Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States' AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

articles.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.
The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.
The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.
And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk.
“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.
The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.
On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.
Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.
In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.
“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said.
Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly, the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.
Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement.
Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.
The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.
“Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

articles.title: Amazon S3 Files
articles.body:
Amazon S3 Files
The first and only cloud object store that provides fully-featured, high-performance file system access to your data
What is S3 Files?
S3 Files is a shared file system that connects any AWS compute directly with your data in Amazon S3. It provides fast, direct access to all of your S3 data as files with full file system semantics and low-latency performance, without your data ever leaving S3. That means file-based applications, agents, and teams can now access and work with S3 data as a file system using the tools they already depend on. You no longer need to duplicate your data or cycle it between object storage and file system storage. Now, file-based tools and applications across your organization can work with your S3 data directly from any compute instance, container, and function using the tools your teams and agents already depend on.
With S3 Files, Amazon S3 is the first and only cloud object store that provides fully-featured, high-performance file system access to your data. S3 Files gives you the performance and simplicity of a file system with the scalability, durability, and cost-effectiveness of S3. There are no data silos, no synchronization complexities, and no tradeoffs. File and object storage, together in one place without compromise.
Benefits
Your applications, agents, and users expect to work with data as files and folders. With S3 Files, everything that needs to work with your S3 data as files can do so directly. Python libraries, ML frameworks, CLI utilities, and shell scripts all work with your S3 data with no custom connectors and no new APIs to learn.
S3 Files delivers low latency and up to multiple terabytes per second of aggregate read throughput. Performance is optimized specifically for file workloads through intelligent caching, minimizing latency and maximizing throughput. S3 Files intelligently loads your active working set onto high-performance storage, delivering low-latency access while keeping costs proportional to what you're actively using.
Organizations duplicate data across storage systems when workflows require both object and file access. S3 Files eliminates duplicate storage and the pipelines required to keep separate systems in sync. Your data lives in S3 and stays in S3, accessible through both file and object interfaces simultaneously. One copy, one place to manage, zero synchronization overhead.
S3 Files is built on S3's pay-as-you-go model with no provisioned capacity and no minimum commitments. Your workload scales automatically within S3 for high-performance, scalable use cases. Storage scales automatically as your data grows, from a single dataset to petabytes, with costs proportional to your active working set and no infrastructure to manage. S3 Files delivers up to 90% lower costs compared to cycling data between S3 and separate file systems.
Data Points
- up to 90% lower costs compared to cycling data between S3 and separate file systems
  90%
- file system IOPS per bucket
  10M+
- multiple terabytes per second of aggregate read throughput
  4TB/s+
- compute resources can simultaneously access the same S3 file system
  25K
How S3 Files works
S3 Files works like a traditional high-performance file system that can be accessed by any Linux-based compute resource, but its view of files and folders reflects what's in your S3 bucket. S3 Files is built using Amazon EFS, which intelligently loads your active working set onto high-performance storage. This delivers low latencies for frequently accessed data while keeping costs proportional to what you're actively using. When you read files, S3 Files lazily loads portions of file metadata and contents onto high-performance storage. Data that doesn't meet your configured file size threshold is read directly from S3, with no file system storage involved. When you write data, your writes are sent to the highly durable high-performance storage and then synced back to S3 to keep your bucket consistent. Data that hasn't been accessed within a configurable window (1 to 365 days, defaulting to 30) automatically expires from this storage, so you pay only for what you're actively using while your authoritative data always remains in S3.
Features and capabilities
Any new or existing S3 bucket can be accessed as a file system, with no data migration required. Your existing file-based applications and tools work exactly as they do today. No code changes, no custom connectors, and no new APIs to learn. Use a prefix to scope exactly what your file-based workloads need, so only your active dataset is placed onto the file system’s high-performance storage. Changes sync automatically back to your S3 bucket. Your full dataset stays in S3, available on demand, while your workloads work with precisely the data they need. With S3 Files, you can perform all file operations through a standard NFS file interface with low latency.
Access the same S3 bucket from multiple compute resources simultaneously through a shared file system. Built for collaboration, S3 Files supports up to 25,000 active connections across any AWS compute resource including Lambda, EC2, ECS, EKS, Fargate, and Batch. They all can read from and write to the same data in real time, with NFS close-to-open consistency. This makes S3 Files ideal for collaborative workloads where multiple users, applications, or agents need shared access to data at the same time.
S3 Files delivers up to 90% lower costs compared to cycling data between S3 and separate file systems. It keeps costs proportional to your active working set by intelligently loading only the data you’re actively using onto high-performance storage. You configure the file size threshold and retention window, and S3 Files automatically manages what stays on high-performance storage versus what’s read directly from S3. For large reads (1 MiB or larger), data is streamed directly from S3 even if it resides on the high-performance storage. Since S3 is optimized for high throughput, these reads incur only standard S3 GET request costs with no file system charge. When you write data, S3 Files batches your writes on the high-performance storage before committing them to S3, reducing S3 request costs. Data that hasn’t been accessed within your configured window automatically expires, so you pay only for what you’re actively using while maintaining complete access to your entire dataset in S3.
S3 Files gives you complete access to your entire S3 bucket through both file and object interfaces simultaneously. Your file-based applications work exactly as they do today. Your object-based applications and workflows continue unchanged. S3 Files intelligently caches the data your file workloads need for high performance, while the full scale, durability, and economics of S3 remain the foundation for your data store. No modifications, no tradeoffs, and nothing to reconcile between two separate systems.
Featured industries
Life Sciences and Healthcare
Life sciences organizations process petabytes of sequencing data from S3 through bioinformatics pipelines that require file system operations to create alignment files, merge results, and update variant calls. Healthcare providers store medical images in S3 and provide file system access for diagnostic workstations and PACS systems. Research organizations enable collaborative analysis of clinical trial data while maintaining S3 as a single source of truth with complete audit trails and regulatory compliance through encryption and access controls.
Financial Services
Quantitative researchers build and test models against petabytes of historical market data, running simulations and backtests that demand shared, low-latency access to live datasets. Maintaining separate local copies of that data created version drift, duplication costs, and slower iteration cycles. With S3 Files, every researcher on the team works from the same live S3 dataset simultaneously, with low latency for intraday risk calculations and results immediately available to every downstream workflow. Research cycles accelerate and the entire team always works from a single source of truth.
Media and Entertainment
Production teams, VFX studios, and render farms depend on file-based tools to access and process footage and assets throughout the production lifecycle. Managing separate storage systems for active production and long-term archival adds cost, complexity, and friction to every project. With S3 Files, artists and editors work directly from S3 with the tools they already use, while the same content remains available via S3 APIs for transcoding and CDN delivery, all from one copy with no synchronization required. Productions move faster and content is always where every workflow needs it.
Manufacturing and Engineering
Engineering teams run CAD workflows that generate and update large files throughout a run, storing results in S3 for long-term retention, version control, and cross-team collaboration. Getting results from simulation tools into S3 for shared access previously required manual transfers and pipeline overhead. With S3 Files, simulation tools write results incrementally to S3 as runs progress, and teams across global locations see updates in real time through a shared mounted bucket. Every iteration is preserved automatically through S3 Versioning, so engineers spend less time managing data and more time iterating on designs.
Use cases
AI agents don’t just read data, they act on it, generate new data, coordinate with other agents, and maintain state across tasks. Agents depend on file-based tools like Python libraries, CLI utilities, and shell scripts, and they need a place to read inputs, write outputs, persist memory and logs, and share intermediate state with other agents in a pipeline. S3 Files gives agents all of that in one place. Each agent accesses the same S3 file system and works with shared data using standard file operations, with no service-specific APIs to learn and no coordination layer to build. S3 becomes the shared operating environment for your entire agent fleet, not just the place data ends up when the work is done.
ML workloads have a specific problem that neither object storage nor traditional file systems alone solve well on their own. Training datasets live in S3 because of its scale and cost, but preprocessing pipelines, feature engineering scripts, and training frameworks all expect to work with files. The result is a copy-and-stage step before every run: pull data from S3, move it to a file system, process it, then push results back. That step adds time, cost, complexity and another failure point to every iteration. S3 Files eliminates this overhead. Data scientists and ML engineers can work with their S3 training data directly through a file system and run their pipelines in place. Preprocessing writes back to the same bucket automatically. Multiple training jobs can read from the same dataset simultaneously without duplication. Faster iterations result in rapid time to quality insights, because the data is always current, always in one place, and always ready to use.
Modern workflows that span applications, users, pipelines, and tools are built to read and write files. They browse directories, open datasets, append results, and save outputs using standard file operations. Connecting these applications to S3 previously required copying data out of S3 first, because S3's API-based model was incompatible with software that expects a file system. S3 Files removes that barrier. Your existing applications mount your S3 file system and work with your data exactly as they do today, with no code changes, no custom connectors, and no data movement. The application does not know it is talking to S3. It just works.
Make your S3 data natively available on any compute resource. With S3 Files, your bucket now appears as a mount to your compute resources, giving researchers, analysts, and data scientists the ability to browse directories, open datasets, run simulations, and save results using the tools they already work with. Your teams access S3 data directly from any compute resource using standard file operations, with all members reading from and writing to the same bucket simultaneously.
Customer quotes
Bayer
Bayer is a global leader in healthcare and nutrition with a mission of "Health for All, Hunger for None." The company develops pharmaceutical treatments and agricultural products intended to address challenges associated with a growing global population. Bayer invests in life sciences research and data-driven approaches with the goal of advancing human health outcomes and supporting sustainable food production practices.
“Bayer's research teams work with enormous volumes of scientific data stored in S3. Before S3 Files, accessing this data meant downloading entire datasets to local storage before analysis could begin. This created delays and required us to maintain additional copies across our research infrastructure. S3 Files simplifies this workflow by letting our data scientists mount S3 data directly as a file system, in accordance with our existing security and access control protocols. Researchers can now open datasets, run analyses, and collaborate on shared results without waiting for downloads or managing data movement. This shift has streamlined our R&D operations and reduced infrastructure overhead, freeing our teams to focus on research and innovation.”
Ben Gonzalez, Senior Cloud Engineer, Bayer
Deloitte
Deloitte is a global leader in professional services, providing consulting, audit, tax, and advisory services across industries with approximately 470,000 professionals across 150 countries.
"As we build AI agent solutions for clients, effective coordination is imperative. Amazon S3 Files is a differentiator that provides our agentic architectures with a shared workspace where agents can retain context, exchange intermediate results, and organize across complex analytics pipelines, all while using standard file operations. With the ability to treat S3 as a local drive for our agents’ logs, state, and checkpoints, this can simplify multi-agent design, sophisticate automation, and accelerate the pace of delivery.”
Chris Jangareddy, Managing Director, AWS Alliance AI and Data Lead, Deloitte Consulting LLP
Cloudsmith
Cloudsmith secures the AI-powered software supply chain. Manage binary artifacts and protect your enterprise from malicious packages and vulnerabilities. Agentic AI development means more software, more dependencies, and more risk. Cloudsmith gives your teams curated repositories of pre-verified artifacts they can build with safely, at AI scale and speed.
"Our platform processes hundreds of thousands of artifacts daily, relying on S3 and file systems to handle complex package processing and synchronization workflows that keep customers’ software supply chains secure. This introduces significant operational overhead, latency, and maintenance complexity. We’re excited about using S3 Files, where our Fargate containers and Lambda functions can access S3 data directly as a file system, eliminating the need for custom synchronization logic. This simplifies our architecture, reduces package time-to-availability for developers, systems, and agents, and preserves compatibility with existing file-based tooling and artifact processing workflows that are critical to our global operations."
Ronan O'Dulaing, VP of Engineering, Cloudsmith
Presidio
Presidio is a premier IT services and solutions provider helping organizations connect today's technology with tomorrow's innovations. As an AWS Premier Consulting Partner, Presidio guides enterprises across financial services, healthcare, and media and entertainment through cloud infrastructure design, deployment, and management.
“Amazon S3 Files advances migration and modernization by connecting object storage with file-based workloads, enabling customers to access S3 data through familiar file interfaces while preserving S3's durability and scalability. For organizations transitioning to AWS, this provides a flexible path to modernizing legacy applications without disruptive rewrites or redundant storage.
At Presidio, we view Amazon S3 Files as a key enabler for AI-driven workloads by consolidating file and object storage into a single foundation that eliminates duplicate systems and operational complexity. This becomes especially powerful as customers advance generative AI, advanced analytics, and agentic use cases, enabling low-latency access to shared datasets and helping teams move efficiently from development to production.”
Ken Ordini, VP of Engineering, Presidio
SciSpace
SciSpace is an agentic AI research platform that helps researchers and students find, read, and write about scientific literature. Every conversation spawns an autonomous agent that searches papers, generates documents, and delivers finished files to the user.
"When an AI agent writes a file, the user expects to open it immediately. At SciSpace, that happens about 27,000 times a day. S3 Files gives every agent session a POSIX file system backed directly by S3, so agents write files with standard operations and users see them seconds later. articles.title: Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms
articles.body:
Suspected Chinese Agents Are Trying to Dupe Americans with Fake Listings on Job Platforms (cnn.com) 13
			
		 	
				"LinkedIn is probably the greatest intelligence tool that's ever been created," CNN heard from Holden Triplett, director of counterintelligence at the National Security Council in the first Trump administration.
A LinkedIn spokesperson responded that "Creating a fake account or misrepresenting your identity is a clear violation of our terms of service."  (And they also told CNN that LinkedIn remains "focused on detecting state-sponsored abuse and will continue to enforce our policies against fake accounts.")  But it's not just happening on LinkedIn...
Suspected Chinese spies have created an elaborate web of fake firms with job opportunities aimed at tricking current and former US officials into divulging government secrets as part of a scheme that is more pervasive than previously reported, CNN has found.  Interviews with a dozen people caught up in the operation — as well as CNN analysis of suspected bogus websites — reveal how there is a much broader target pool for obtaining sensitive US information after the Trump administration laid off thousands of federal employees. [CNN reported in 2025 that "foreign powers such as China and Russia" had directed their intelligence services "to ramp up recruiting of Americans working in national security by targeting those who had been fired or felt they were at risk of losing their jobs".] These workers left their posts with inadequate guidance and protection from spying plots, ex-officials said, creating a potentially valuable resource for Beijing and weak spot for Washington...  In addition to government workers, the plot has targeted journalists, trade consultants and others, who might have knowledge deemed valuable to US adversaries.
The FBI offered a glimpse into the malicious recruiting scam when it seized 13 websites officials say were tied to fake consulting firms in June. China denied the FBI allegations. CNN analyzed the sites' software code, looked at other suspicious job listings, and interviewed people approached by similar companies. CNN identified several more websites that mimicked the style and substance of those disabled by the FBI.   Two more sites that Max Lesser, a senior analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, discovered and shared with CNN have some of the same web infrastructure or other connections to the seized websites.  In total, Lesser has uncovered more than 100 other web domains, many of which share similar characteristics with the sites taken down by the FBI....
This sprawling network has the hallmarks of a Chinese intelligence operation, Lesser told CNN.  
After creating fake web sites, the operatives "plant vague, well-paying job ads for consulting positions focused on China-related issues" on jobs sites like LinkedIn, CNN reports, asking applicants to produce "research reports". ("[D]ozens or hundreds of such reports, across various topics of interest to Beijing, can start to form a much clearer picture of US national security policy and its vulnerabilities, according to current and former FBI officials.")
CNN sent a detailed request for a comment to a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC.  "I am not familiar with what you mentioned," they responded, adding that China "opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called 'Chinese spy' narrative."

articles.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1M orbital data center satellites
articles.body:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

articles.title: How Can Anything Beat n log n?
articles.body:
How Can Anything Beat n log n?
Section: Home / Post
Categories: Computer Science,
Tags: Algorithms, Entropy, Information Theory,
Recently, headlines have kept making the rounds about sub-$n \log n$ algorithms—first Duan et al. breaking Dijkstra’s $O(m + n \log n)$ sorting barrier for directed shortest paths, and then a preprint claiming sub-$n \log n$ integer multiplication.
My first reaction was skepticism. If a problem cares about ordering $n$ items, don’t you need $\log n$ steps to uniquely place each item, repeated $n$ times? That gives $n \log n$. How could you possibly do better?
The short answer is that $n \log n$ is not a universal speed limit. It is the lower bound of a specific model of computation. To see how algorithms beat it, we need to look at what $n \log n$ actually measures—and which assumptions those algorithms drop.
What $n \log n$ Actually Looks Like
Think of sorting $n$ items as routing each item down a decision tree into its final slot.
If you are only allowed to take 2-way comparison steps (< or >), every fork in the tree has 2 branches. Each step cuts the remaining slots in half. To route one item to its unique leaf among $n$ slots, it has to travel down roughly $\log_2 n$ levels.
Send all $n$ items down a tree of depth $\log_2 n$, and you pay $n \log_2 n$ total steps.
The Hidden Assumptions
That intuition feels airtight: if characterizing or placing a single item among $n$ slots takes $\log_2 n$ steps, and there are $n$ items to process, then any task requiring ordering or classification across $n$ items seems forced to pay $n \log_2 n$. Under two specific conditions, that reasoning is airtight:
- Black-box items: You cannot peek inside an item. Your only tool is a 2-way yes/no step (like is a < b?) that yields at most 1 bit of information per step.
- Factorial-scale outcomes: The number of possible final answers grows like $n!$ (or $n^n$)—meaning each of the $n$ items could end up in one of roughly $n$ distinct roles or positions. Not every task on $n$ items has that many outcomes: finding the maximum has only $n$ possible answers and assigning yes/no labels has $2^n$, compared to $n!$ orderings for sorting.
How Existing Algorithms Break $n \log n$
Counterexamples already exist in every algorithms textbook. Two classic ones—Bucket Sort and Radix Sort—sort $n$ numbers in $O(n)$ time when the numbers come from a bounded range or fixed digit width:
- Bucket Sort computes a bucket address directly from each number’s value, drops the item straight into that bucket in a single step (when numbers map cleanly into $n$ slots, that is a direct $n$-way lookup), and then reads the buckets back in order.
- Radix Sort processes numbers one digit at a time. In Most-Significant-Digit (MSD) Radix Sort, 3-digit numbers are first routed into 10 buckets (0–9) by their hundreds digit; only buckets holding more than one item are split again by their tens digit, and so on—without ever comparing two numbers against each other.
Neither algorithm breaks mathematics. Both drop the black-box assumption—and flatten the tree.
Imagine lining up 30 kids by birth month. If you treat them as black boxes and only compare pairs of kids (“who was born earlier?”), you are stuck with a 2-way tree of depth $\log_2 n$. Instead, put 12 labeled boxes on the floor (Jan through Dec). Each kid looks at their own birth month and walks straight to their box in one step.
Computers can do the same thing because numbers aren’t opaque black boxes—they are digits and bit patterns, and hardware can jump directly to a memory address in a single step. Direct indexing widens the branching factor all the way to $n$, collapsing the tree to depth 1. MSD Radix Sort makes the intermediate case just as clear: it routes the exact same items down a tree, except each node has 10 branches (0–9) instead of 2, flattening the depth from $\log_2 n$ down to the number of digits—with zero comparisons. (As we will see next, when numbers are allowed to grow arbitrarily large with $n$, escaping $n \log n$ asymptotically requires choosing the branching factor as a function of $n$ rather than keeping it fixed at 10.)
The Information-Theoretic View
Why does widening the branching factor break $n \log n$, and when is a lower bound truly unavoidable? Information theory puts both assumptions into a single equation.
In an earlier post on entropy, I framed entropy $H$ as the minimum number of binary choices (bits) needed to describe categories of events:
$$ H(\text{outcomes}) = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i $$
That same lens gives us a hard floor for any algorithm.
Let $N$ be the total number of possible final answers to a problem—a function of the input size $n$, not $n$ itself. When every answer is equally likely (the worst case, $p_i = 1/N$), the entropy of the answer space simplifies to:
$$ H(N) = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{N} \log_2 \frac{1}{N} = \log_2 N $$
Why is $H(N) = \log_2 N$ a hard floor for 2-way steps? Let $q$ be the number of 2-way (yes/no) steps an algorithm takes. Those $q$ steps can produce at most $2^q$ distinct transcripts of answers. If $2^q < N$, at least two different final answers must share the exact same transcript, and no algorithm can tell them apart. Therefore:
$$ 2^q \ge N \implies q \ge \log_2 N = H(N) $$
Where does the $\log_2 n$ in $n \log_2 n$ come from? Logarithms turn multiplication into addition:
- When each item has 2 outcomes ($N = 2^n$), taking the log yields $H(2^n) = \log_2(2^n) = n$—linear, with no $\log n$.
- When all $n$ items can be ordered in $N = n!$ ways, you are multiplying $n$ factors that grow with $n$. Taking $H(n!) = \log_2(n!)$ adds up $\log_2 1 + \log_2 2 + \dots + \log_2 n$, which lands at roughly $n \log_2 n$.
Now look at what happens when you widen each step’s branching factor to $k$. Remember from the entropy post that the base of the logarithm corresponds to how many outcomes a single step can distinguish, so $q$ $k$-way steps yield $k^q$ transcripts:
$$ k^q \ge N \implies q \ge \frac{H(N)}{\log_2 k} = \log_k N $$
Notice a crucial distinction here. Any constant $k$-way step only differs from a 2-way step by a constant factor ($1/\log_2 k$): a fixed 10-way decimal lookup trims the work by $\log_2 10 \approx 3.32\times$, and a fixed 256-way byte lookup trims it by $8\times$, yet as $n$ grows without bound (and distinct numbers need at least $\log_k n$ digits), both stay locked to $O(n \log n)$ forever.
To actually escape $n \log n$, $k$ must be a function of $n$ (for example, $k = \sqrt{n}$ or $k = n$). Once $k$ scales with $n$ as $k = n^\alpha$, $\log_2 k = \alpha \log_2 n$ cancels the $\log_2 n$ in $n \log_2 n$, so the total number of steps is only off from a one-shot $n$-way lookup by a constant factor ($1/\alpha$)—that is, linear $O(n)$. Radix Sort achieves this when its base $k$ is chosen relative to the size and range of the numbers (e.g., $k = n$ or $k = \sqrt{n}$): we are using the numerical value of the input itself to inform the algorithm’s addressing, piercing the black box.
Entropy Is a Floor, Not a Guarantee
One important nuance: having $H(N) = \log_2 N$ bits of entropy does not guarantee you can solve a problem in $\log_2 N$ steps (or $\log_k N$ steps with a $k$-way step).
Compare searching a sorted list against finding the maximum of an unsorted list. Both have $N = n$ possible answers, so both have the exact same entropy: $H(n) = \log_2 n$ bits. Yet finding the max takes $n - 1$ comparisons, because each step only knocks out one loser—it cannot cut the remaining candidates in half.
More generally, to reach $q \approx \log_k N = H(N) / \log_2 k$ steps with a $k$-way step over $N$ possible outcomes, each step must partition the remaining candidates symmetrically (evenly) into $k$ disjoint buckets of roughly $N/k$ outcomes. That is what lets every step shrink the answer space by division ($N \to N/k$) and extract the full $\log_2 k$ bits toward the answer.
When a step is asymmetric—say, checking “is item $i$ the target?” on an unsorted list, where one branch isolates $1$ outcome and the other leaves $N - 1$—the worst-case branch shrinks by subtraction ($N \to N - 1$) instead of division, so you never reach $\log_k N$. Finding the maximum runs into a related failure: a > b has two equally likely outcomes, yet on the answer space of $N$ candidate maxima it only discards a single loser, leaving $N - 1$ candidates alive either way because the remaining information is spent on relative order we do not need. You only hit the entropy floor when the problem’s structure lets each step carve the remaining answers into roughly equal, disjoint fractions.
Bringing It All Together
Every complexity claim sits on two axes: how fast the answer space $N$ grows, and how much information a single $k$-way step can extract.
So whenever you see a headline announcing a sub-$n \log n$ algorithm, there are only two ways it happened: either the problem never actually had a factorial-scale answer space in the first place (computing shortest-path distances doesn’t require sorting every vertex, and multiplying two $n$-bit integers only has $2^{2n}$ possible outputs—an entropy floor of $2n$, never $n!$), or the algorithm found a way to look inside the box and widen the branching factor $k$ with $n$.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
Posted on November 25, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 1 Comment
Real life mythos and legends often play a role in creating a fantasy world 0f one’s own, and author Alma Alexander has an especially unique myth0logy (one that is personal to her) that she is drawing from for the first book in her new trilogy, The Shadow Before the Dawn.
ALMA ALEXANDER:
Back in the 12th century, a quondam poet wrote an epic that contained the line, “There are only three subject matters for any discerning man: that of France, that of Britain, and that of Great Rome.” Possibly the most immediately familiar one of these would be the Matter of Britain – you will know it as the body of medieval literature associated with Great and with Less Britain (Brittany, for those who recognize it better by that name), and concerned with the legendary kings and heroes associated with it, King Arthur, Lancelot, the Knights of the Round Table, the Holy Grail, all that (mostly, blame Geoffrey of Monmouth). The Matter of France deals with Charlemagne and his paladins, and their wars with Moors and Saracens. The Matter of Rome, or Res Romana, is a more rarefied elixir of Greek and Roman mythology, which includes the Matter of Troy (hence the Odyssey and the Iliad), and which focused on military heroes like Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.
But although those three were “anointed”, as it were, there are very much other “Matters” out there, for various countries and cultures. We might argue about whether Wagner muddied the waters with the Ring of the Nibelungen and twisted Matters of Norse origin and of German origin together in a Gordian knot; the Matter of Spain could be – well – maybe El Cid (Spanish people, feel free to correct me); we might definitely argue about the Matter of America, and about ideas it might contain, such as Manifest Destiny. The Matters of Countries are the invisible backbones upon which the shape of their existence hangs.
There is a Matter hidden deep in Eastern Europe, my own Matter, which talks of a line of Kings who walked into being a line of Saints, who created a kingdom out of a smattering of feeble little fiefdoms, and then forged it into an empire, and then fought a Last Battle in which everything they wrought in the Earthly realm was destroyed but which wrote their lineage into the Heavenly ledgers forever and gave their people the light they needed in order to survive the 500 years of slavery that followed their loss in that Last Battle. I am talking about the Nemanjic Dynasty in the 12th/13th centuries Balkans.
For a long time I have wanted to go back to that ancient tree and pick its fruit. This is my own Matter, the one that belongs to my own background, to my own people. It is a period stuffed with history, mystery, miracles, myths, legends, and larger-than-life characters, ripe for the plucking, and one which is rather less well known to the English-language reading public than the more easily accessible Matters out there. I started on a version of this story years ago, and wrote about 20,000 words of it, and then Life fell on me like a landslide and I lost in quick succession my husband, my mother, and a 19-year-old cat (don’t just dismiss this last; I had raised her from a 9-week-old kitten who weighed less than what it would take to make a decent hamburger when she came into my hands, and her loss HURT).
For six years I was a caregiver and then (in increasingly dense layers) someone who mourned and grieved, and all of that leaves little room for telling stories… so I kind of stopped writing. At all. And then, somehow, I picked up those twenty thousand words and looked at them again. And realized that I needed to tell another story before the story that I set out to tell in the first place. And then I realized that I needed to tell another story before THAT, to give weight and stability to the Matter I was addressing. And just like that, I had a trilogy on my hands.
The Shadow Before the Dawn, book 1 in what became that trilogy, was finally fully formed in 2026. The other books are in process. But that first book… this story matters to me, right from that beginning, deeply, organically. Sometimes I think everything I have ever written was training for this story, these books, to which I feel a true responsibility and which I am dedicated to giving the respect and dignity that they deserve.
Because I am writing a Matter. A story that shaped a nation.
You might not know this story.
Come with me, and let me open the doors into a world full of a magic which may be rich and strange and unfamiliar to you. It isn’t to me. This is my Matter, and it runs in my blood. I hope, when you are done reading this, that you will judge that I have done justice to it.
The Shadow Before the Dawn: Amazon

articles.title: Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds
articles.body:
Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds (apnews.com) 15
			
		 	
				The Associated Press reports:
A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.  But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying.  Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. 
The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.  In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September...
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.

articles.title: 72-Hour Fasting Can Reset Your Immune System, USC Study Shows
articles.body:
The USC-led research behind this headline investigated how prolonged fasting and refeeding affected blood-forming stem cells, mainly in mice. Published in Cell Stem Cell on June 5, 2014, it also included preliminary observations from cancer patients receiving chemotherapy.
It did not demonstrate that a single 72-hour fast resets the entire immune system in healthy people. The distinction between mouse regeneration experiments and early human observations is essential to understanding what the paper actually established.
The work remains scientifically interesting because it connected nutrient-sensitive signaling with the behavior of hematopoietic stem cells. These cells help replenish blood and immune-cell populations throughout life.
But a mechanism worth studying is not the same as an established self-treatment. This article examines the original findings, the later human feasibility study and why the word reset can obscure important limits in the evidence.
The immune system is not a single object
The immune system comprises many kinds of cells, tissues and communication pathways. Blood measurements capture part of that system, but they do not provide a complete inventory of every immune cell or its function.
Some cells circulate, while others reside in tissues or move between compartments. A change in the number found in blood can reflect movement as well as production, survival or loss.
That is why fewer circulating cells cannot automatically be interpreted as the removal of old or damaged cells. Likewise, a later increase does not by itself prove that every returning cell has been newly generated.
Immune health also depends on more than cell counts. The ability to respond to infection, maintain useful immune memory and avoid harmful inflammation involves coordinated activity across many populations.
A strong research claim should specify which part of the system was measured and which outcome improved. A complete reset would require a far broader demonstration than a change in white blood cell measurements.
The 2014 study’s focus was the hematopoietic system, especially the response of blood-forming stem cells to experimental stress. That is a substantial topic without expanding it into every feature of human immunity.
What hematopoietic stem cells do
Hematopoietic stem cells are cells with the capacity to maintain themselves and generate the precursors of different blood-cell lineages. They are supported by a local environment often called their niche.
The balance between self-renewal and differentiation matters. A stem-cell population needs to preserve its long-term capacity while producing the cells required for ongoing function.
Aging and injury can alter that balance. Researchers study whether changes in signaling or environment shift the kinds of cells produced, their resilience or their ability to recover after damage.
In this setting, the word regeneration refers to restoring or replenishing aspects of a blood-forming system. It does not necessarily mean replacing every immune cell or erasing a person’s immune history.
Experiments can investigate these processes using cell markers, functional assays and comparisons between treated and control animals. These methods provide more specific information than a simple before-and-after blood count.
However, findings from such experiments still need to be translated carefully. Mouse stem-cell behavior under a defined protocol is not a direct measurement of what happens after an unsupervised fast in an adult human.
What the USC experiment found
The researchers investigated repeated cycles of prolonged fasting and refeeding in mice, including animals exposed to chemotherapy. Their analyses examined blood-cell populations, stem cells and molecular signals related to growth and stress responses.
They reported that fasting reduced circulating IGF-1 and activity in a pathway involving protein kinase A, or PKA. These changes were associated with altered stem-cell behavior and recovery in the experimental setting.
The study also used manipulations of the proposed signaling pathway to investigate mechanism. That is important because changing a candidate pathway can provide stronger evidence than simply observing that it moves alongside an outcome.
The authors reported protection against chemotherapy-related suppression of the hematopoietic system and changes in age-associated lineage balance in mice. The experimental conclusions concern particular models, treatments and measured outcomes.
They do not establish that every cause of immune dysfunction responds the same way. Aging, chemotherapy exposure, infection, autoimmune disease and inherited immune disorders are biologically different contexts.
Nor should experimental fasting durations in mice be converted directly into a universal human schedule. Species differ in metabolism and physiology, so matching hours does not necessarily match biological exposure.
Refeeding was part of the experimental cycle
The study examined cycles rather than an uninterrupted fast considered in isolation. Recovery after food was reintroduced was relevant to the reported replenishment of blood-cell populations.
This matters because a headline can make the period without food sound like the entire intervention. In reality, the physiological response can change between nutrient deprivation and the return of nutrients.
A cell under limited nutrient availability may alter growth, maintenance or stress-response pathways. The subsequent availability of nutrients can support a different set of activities, including proliferation and replenishment.
That sequence is a biological hypothesis to test, not a reason to improvise a protocol. The timing, nutritional context and health of the organism can all affect the response.
Studying a cycle also requires more than taking one blood sample at the end of a fast. Measurements at several points help distinguish a transient shift from a persistent change in production or function.
The research therefore supports interest in the interaction between metabolic state and regeneration. It does not establish a universal moment at which an entire immune system switches from old to new.
What the early human observations could show
The 2014 paper included preliminary hematological observations from a phase 1 study of fasting around platinum-based chemotherapy. It compared observations associated with fasting periods of different lengths.
The authors described findings consistent with protection of some blood-cell measures in the longer-fasting group. They also explicitly stated that these preliminary results needed expansion and confirmation.
This was not a demonstration that healthy volunteers regenerated their whole immune systems. It was a small early clinical investigation in a specific oncology setting, with different chemotherapy combinations among participants.
Phase 1 research commonly asks whether an approach is feasible and tolerable under selected conditions. Such work can identify signals that justify later studies without proving that the intervention improves long-term health.
Patients undergoing chemotherapy are also not interchangeable with the general population. Their treatment, illness, nutritional status and clinical monitoring create circumstances different from those of someone experimenting at home.
Those distinctions should remain visible whenever the human portion of the study is described. Calling it a human trial does not automatically give it the power or scope of a large randomized efficacy study.
The later feasibility report involved 20 patients
A 2016 BMC Cancer report examined the safety and feasibility of fasting in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy in 20 participants. Its purpose and selected population are central to its interpretation.
The investigators excluded patients with diabetes, low body mass index or substantial recent weight loss. Those exclusions are evidence that safety could not simply be assumed for all cancer patients.
The participants also received care within a study framework. Clinical selection and monitoring are part of the conditions under which an experimental dietary intervention is evaluated.
A small study can provide information about common short-term problems and practical adherence. It is less capable of detecting uncommon harms or establishing durable improvements in cancer outcomes, infection resistance or longevity.
The report therefore should not be presented as confirmation that the entire immune system was rebuilt. It addressed a narrower clinical development question and described measurements within that context.
Its findings are relevant to further research, but they do not authorize changing an oncology treatment plan. Nutritional decisions during cancer care can have consequences that require individualized clinical judgment.
Why an immune-cell count is not a functional reset
White blood cell counts are useful clinical measurements, especially during treatments that can suppress blood-cell production. They do not capture every dimension of immune competence.
Two people can have similar counts while differing in the composition, activation state or function of their immune cells. Tissue-resident populations and immune memory add further complexity.
Similarly, a count returning toward baseline after an intervention does not establish that the resulting cells are superior to the earlier population. Demonstrating improved function requires relevant tests and outcomes.
For a proposed infection benefit, researchers would need evidence concerning infections or validated measures of protective responses. For a proposed aging benefit, they would need outcomes appropriate to health and function over time.
The term reset combines these different possibilities into an appealing image. Scientific evaluation needs to separate them so each can be tested rather than assumed.
Other fasting research shows context matters
A 2019 Cell study of dietary intake and inflammatory monocytes investigated how nutrient availability affects circulating immune-cell populations. It illustrates that diet can alter immune distribution and activity without implying universal rejuvenation.
Monocytes are one part of immunity, and changing their presence in blood can have several biological meanings. The relationship between inflammation and host defense depends on the setting.
Reducing excessive inflammatory activity may be useful in one context while weakening an appropriate response could be harmful in another. More immune activation and less immune activation are not automatically better or worse.
This is one reason claims about boosting immunity need precision. A useful intervention should improve a specified outcome rather than merely moving a marker in a direction described as favorable.
It also explains why distinct fasting protocols should not be merged casually. Short-term restriction, time-restricted eating, repeated prolonged fasting and fasting-mimicking diets are different exposures.
Evidence for one cannot establish the effectiveness of all the others. Calories, nutrients, timing and participant characteristics can influence whether the underlying biology is comparable.
What the study does not establish about aging
The immune system changes with age, and hematopoietic stem cells are relevant to those changes. That makes the USC work of interest to geroscience, the study of biological processes associated with aging.
However, an intervention that changes lineage balance in old mice does not automatically extend healthy lifespan in humans. That requires a separate chain of evidence.
Aging is also not a single process. A shift in blood-forming cells cannot establish that damage in the brain, cardiovascular system, muscles or other tissues has been reversed.
The study is therefore best understood as an investigation of particular pathways and outcomes. It contributes to a larger research program rather than providing a complete treatment for aging.
The original publication is from 2014, not a new clinical breakthrough in 2026. Its age does not make it irrelevant, but readers should know when the evidence was produced and how preliminary the human claims were.
Safety cannot be inferred from the word natural
Going without food for an extended period changes nutrient availability and can interact with illness, medications and an individual’s nutritional reserves. Those interactions make prolonged fasting a medical consideration rather than a universally benign experiment.
People receiving cancer treatment may already face appetite problems, weight loss or difficulty maintaining adequate nutrition. A strategy tolerable in selected study participants may be inappropriate for someone with different risks.
The exclusions in the feasibility study make that limitation concrete. A result from a group selected to avoid certain vulnerabilities cannot establish safety in the very groups excluded.
The same reasoning applies beyond oncology. Pregnancy, growth, frailty, metabolic disease and a history of disordered eating create circumstances that cannot be reduced to an internet fasting timetable.
This article is not a fasting protocol. Someone considering prolonged restriction, particularly during treatment for an illness, needs advice from a clinician who can assess their specific circumstances.
Importantly, fasting is not a replacement for chemotherapy, vaccination, infection treatment or other established care. The USC research does not support stopping those interventions in pursuit of an immune reset.
How commercial claims can outrun the evidence
The paper disclosed that senior author Valter Longo had an equity interest in L-Nutra, a company developing medical food. Such disclosures are part of the context readers should have when evaluating potential applications.
A financial relationship does not automatically invalidate the experiments. It does make it important to distinguish the research intervention from claims about commercial programs or products.
The study cannot establish that every fasting-mimicking product reproduces its mouse findings. A different formulation, duration or participant population requires its own evidence.
Likewise, a product described as activating fasting pathways may not produce the same exposure or biological effect. A marketing analogy to a mechanism is not a clinical outcome.
Independent studies, prespecified analyses and complete reporting help evaluate whether a promising idea translates reliably. They are particularly important when the public claim becomes broader than the original experiment.
What a decisive human trial would need to measure
A stronger human study would first define its intended population and goal. Protecting selected patients from treatment-related blood-cell suppression is different from improving vaccine responses or reducing infections in older adults.
The intervention would need a clear description, with appropriate nutritional assessment and monitoring. A comparison group would help distinguish its effects from normal recovery, treatment variation and other changes over time.
Researchers should specify clinical outcomes in advance. Blood counts could contribute to the evidence, but a claim about whole-system improvement would need broader functional measurements.
Longer observation would help establish durability and detect delayed harms. It would also show whether any short-term signal translates into a benefit that matters in everyday life.
Studies should report who was excluded as clearly as who participated. That allows clinicians and readers to understand the boundaries of both the safety findings and the proposed benefit.
Finally, replication matters. An early signal becomes more persuasive when independent teams can reproduce it and when later trials address the uncertainties left by the initial study.
Separating a change from a benefit
When evaluating any dietary experiment, it helps to ask what the measurement actually represents. A lower concentration, a different cell ratio and a change in gene activity are observations; their meaning depends on the biological and clinical context.
The next question is whether the change lasts after ordinary conditions resume. Temporary adaptation can be scientifically informative without demonstrating a lasting improvement in health.
The final question is whether a person fares better because of it. That requires outcomes such as fewer complications or improved function, evaluated in a way that can distinguish treatment effects from chance and alternative explanations.
A valuable mechanism without a proven human reset
The USC work connected fasting-related signaling with blood-forming stem-cell behavior in experimental models. It provided a scientific rationale for further investigation of protection and regeneration in particular settings.
The human evidence in the original report was preliminary, and the later small feasibility study did not establish universal immune regeneration. The supplied headline should be read with that central limitation in mind.
The useful question is not whether a three-day countdown guarantees a new immune system. It is which nutrient-sensitive mechanisms can be modified safely to improve a defined outcome in a defined group.
Keeping that question specific preserves the research’s value. It supports continued investigation without turning an intriguing mouse finding into an unsupported promise or a potentially risky instruction.
The human feasibility design also raises an important comparison problem. If groups follow different fasting durations and receive different chemotherapy combinations, a difference in blood-cell recovery may have more than one explanation. Larger randomized studies can help disentangle those factors.
Selection and adherence require attention as well. People able to complete a restrictive protocol may differ from those who cannot, including in nutritional reserves or illness severity. An analysis that overlooks those differences can overstate how widely a result applies.
For that reason, a complete clinical report should describe withdrawals, deviations and adverse experiences alongside the most encouraging measurements. Understanding who could not follow an intervention is part of evaluating it, especially when the proposed strategy involves restricting nutrition during a demanding treatment.
Featured image: illustrative photograph by manu schwendener on Unsplash, under the Unsplash License. It is not a recommendation to undertake prolonged fasting.
