articles.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
articles.body:
Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.
According to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”
But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.
Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.
The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.
404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.
Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.
Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.
The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

articles.title: S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised
articles.body:
S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised (usnews.com)
			
		 	
				S&P Global Ratings has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on downgrade watch, warning that Jensen Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement as CEO exposed weaknesses in the company's corporate governance and board oversight. "We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said. Reuters reports:  Nvidia currently has an 'AA' rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is 'AAA'. The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects. Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker. The agency said Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook remain unaffected, but added that governance and regulatory uncertainty persists.

articles.title: December 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
articles.body:
December 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeatured
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit. 
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.
Bryson County Retreat Featured
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
Deadline: Rolling.
Open Calls
Wildlife Photographer of the Year(International)
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.
Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art(International)
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for This Memory, a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead. 
Deadline: December 4, 2026.
Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab(Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.
Material Works Art Award 2026(International)
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.
Call for Mail Art(International)
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition love|mark, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.
Sony Future Filmmaker Awards(International)
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.
GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals(International)
Olbrich Botanical Gardens in Madison, Wisconsin, invites proposals for temporary, large-scale, light-based artwork for GLEAM, a public art exhibition. The show will be open to the public from August 28 to October 23, 2027.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. CST on January 6, 2027.
Visual Arts Prize IDEA – Vila d’Amer(International)
Apply for this inaugural prize open to artists working in all visual arts media. Two winning artworks, with prizes of €3,500 and €1,500, will become part of the permanent International Visual Arts Collection IDEA – Vila d’Amer.
Deadline: January 10, 2027.
360 CHICAGO: CloudWalk Call for Artists(Chicago)
One artist will be selected for this major installation in the CloudWalk gallery atop 875 N. Michigan Ave. The selected artist receives a $10,000 commission, and the winning installation will go on view starting April 2027.
Deadline: January 18, 2027.
World of WearableArt 2027 Competition(International)
Entries are now open for the 2027 WOW Competition in Wellington, New Zealand. Awards consist of NZ$200,000 in prizes, including the Supreme WOW Award of NZ$30,000.
Deadline: February 11, 2027 (international), March 31, 2027 (New Zealand).
Grants
The Filmed in Nevada County Grant(International)
To support filmmakers in the production of work in Nevada County, California, Nevada City Film Festival offers grants between $1,000 and $20,000.
Deadline: December 1, 2026.
Southern Prize and State Fellowships for Visual Arts(U.S. South)
The South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowships acknowledge the highest quality artistic work being created in the American South. The program is open to individual artists living in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. State Fellowships are $5,000, with one awarded per state. These then compete for two Southern Prize tiers of $25,000 and $10,000.
Deadline: January 15, 2027 (fee waiver request by December 18, 2026).
The Virigina A. Groot Foundation Grants(International)
Each year, the Virginia A. Groot Foundation offers three grants to artists who have exceptional talent and a demonstrated ability in ceramic sculpture or sculpture of diverse mediums. The grants are organized into tiers, with the top award providing $60,000, the second award offering $30,000, and the third awarding $20,000.
Deadline: January 9, 2027.
Foundation for Contemporary Arts Emergency Grants(U.S.)
Emergency Grants provide urgent funding for visual and performing artists and poets who have sudden, unanticipated opportunities to present their work to the public, but there is insufficient time to seek other sources of funding or unexpected expenses are incurred for projects close to completion. Each month, the organization makes approximately 15 to 20 grants in the range of $500 to $3,000 each.
Deadline: Rolling.
National Lottery Project Grants(U.K.)
Both individuals and organizations can apply to Arts Council National Lottery Project Grants. These awards are designed to focus on specific projects with starting and ending dates including festivals and carnivals, dance, libraries, literature, museums, music, theater, or visual arts programs. There is no maximum threshold for the fund.
Deadline: Rolling.
Black Artists Grant(U.K.)
The Black Artists Grant offered by Creative Debuts is no-strings-attached financial support to help Black artists. Selected applicants receive £500, and applications are reviewed monthly.
Deadline: Rolling.
The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)
This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.
Deadline: Rolling.
Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)
The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.
Deadline: Rolling.
Residencies, Fellowships, & More
Kent Cultural Alliance Spring 2027 SERVICE Residency(U.S.)
Artists are invited to apply for a six-week residency session in Chestertown, Maryland, devoted to the theme of service. Each selected artist will receive a $7,500 stipend for the six-week session, a travel reimbursement up to $1,000, and studio and gallery expense reimbursement up to $1,500.
Deadline: 5 p.m. EST on December 1, 2026.
Charles Allis Art Museum Artist in Residence(International)
Located in Milwaukee’s Lower East Side neighborhood, the Charles Allis Art Museum residency program gives one artist the opportunity to engage with the Allis’ collection of more than 800 historic pieces from the early 20th century. The participant receives an $1,800 honorarium and up to a $400 travel stipend.
Deadline: December 4, 2026.
2026 McKnight Fellowships for Fiber Artists(Minnesota)
Each year, the Textile Center awards two unrestricted $25,000 fellowships to post-emerging Minnesota fiber artists who demonstrate exceptional proficiency, sustained practice, and commitment to the field. Fellowship dates are March 1, 2027, to February 28, 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.
Open AIR Residencies(International)
Open AIR is a Missoula-based nonprofit that brings artists and communities together through place-based residencies and public arts programs across Montana. Sessions currently accepting applications include summer 2027, fall 2027, and spring 2028.
Deadline: December 7, 2026.
Cove Park Awarded Residencies for 2027-28(International)
Located in beautiful Argyll & Bute, Scotland, Cove Park awards funded residencies, in addition to travel, visa, materials, and access allowances when required. (Self-funded Open Residencies and subsidized winter residencies are open on a rolling basis.)
Deadline: December 11, 2026.
An Talla Solais Càirdeas/The Kinship Residency(International)
BIPOC artists working in any medium are invited to apply to this fully funded residency in Ullapool in the Scottish Highlands. The program runs throughout January, February, and March 2027. The residency covers all work space, housing, mentoring, and exhibition costs in addition to a £750 weekly stipend.
Deadline: December 14, 2026.
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency 2027-28(International)
Joshua Tree Highlands Artist Residency offers time and space amidst the natural beauty of Joshua Tree National Park. Seven-week residencies include scholarship funds, housing, and studio space designed to accommodate a broad range of artistic activity and open studio events. There is a $45 application fee.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.
ren AiR(International)
ren is a discovery platform where you share everything that goes into your artistic practice. For its residency, four selected artists will each receive $5,000 to develop and realize a project of their choice, wherever they are based, while sharing their creative journey with the ren community. In addition, eight artists will receive $2,000 prizes.
Deadline: December 31, 2026.
Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship(International)
The Ox-Bow Summer Fellowship offers twelve weeks to slow down and deepen your practice within a creative community. The program will welcome 18 fellows and is open to senior BFA students, MFA students, postgraduates, and artists with comparable professional experience.
Deadline: January 7, 2027.
Fine Arts Work Center Seven-Month Residency(International)
The Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown grants 10 annual fellowships each to visual artists and writers for a seven-month residency that runs from October 1 to April 30. Visual arts fellows are provided with a private furnished apartment and a separate studio, a $1,300 monthly stipend, plus a $1,000 exit stipend to support relocation at the end of the fellowship. There is a $55 application fee until midday on December 1, then $65 until the opportunity closes.
Deadline: February 6, 2027.
Smithereen Farm Winter Residency(International)
Smithereen Farm offers affordable, shared, winter housing to farmers and agrarian-adjacent people and creatives. In the winter, its studio spaces and rooms in shared houses are generally rented for $350 per month, which includes access to common rooms, space for studio work or desks, utilities, fast Wi-Fi at Reversing Hall, a carpenter shop, sewing machines, video projection space, and access to the farm’s agricultural library.
Deadline: Rolling.
Jackrabbit Studios Residency(International)
Jackrabbit Studios is a creative sanctuary and retreat space in the Southern California High Desert that welcomes creatives, healing arts practitioners, and facilitators at any stage of practice to our five acres of secluded and sublime desert expanse to craft a residency tailored to your season of practice. Fees range from $450 per week to $2,000 per week, and pets are welcome for an additional fee.
Deadline: Rolling.

articles.title: Qualcomm's Oryon 3 Reaches the Top
articles.body:
Qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.
The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.
Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.
Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the new core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.
A Faster Frontend
Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.
Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.
High core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.
Compared to AMD and Intel’s latest cores, Qualcomm lacks any ability to handle more than one taken branch per cycle. Arm’s newer cores are also capable of doing two taken branches per cycle. I suspect AMD, Arm, and Intel decided that handling multiple taken branches per cycle became more profitable once their cores got wide enough, so seeing Qualcomm build a very wide core without that ability is surprising. Perhaps clock speed factors into that decision, because going from 4.3 to 5 GHz is a huge jump. If so, Qualcomm’s choice would be justified because a clock speed increase of that magnitude probably offers a larger performance increase than going for two taken branches per cycle. Of course, it’s impossible to know if branch predictor paths presented a timing challenge for Oryon.
For branches with dynamic taken/not-taken behavior, Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle conditional predictor. Testing with branches whose outcomes correlate with increasingly long history lengths shows an average 0.5 cycle increase in time per branch over an always- taken reference run, as long as the test stays within the conditional predictor’s capabilities. Because I randomly generate patterns so that each branch is taken roughly 50% of the time, a 0.5 cycle average penalty suggests Qualcomm only incurs the 2-cycle timing if the direction predictor disagrees with a base prediction. Direction prediction starts falling apart with more than 32K patterns in play, which is an improvement over the approximately 24K patterns that first generation Oryon could handle in this test.
For comparison, Zen 5’s conditional predictor can handle roughly 48K patterns before falling apart. Unlike Oryon 3, and unlike some older Zen generations, Zen 5 does not show an increase in branch latency compared to an always-taken pattern.
Indirect branches can go to multiple targets, and present another level of difficulty because the branch predictor has to select between previously seen targets, and must store more than one target per branch. Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle indirect predictor that can track 2048 indirect targets, matching its predecessor.
A single branch can jump to 256 targets without incurring a significant penalty. This could mean at least eight of the bits that Oryon 3 uses to index into its indirect target array are influenced by branch history.
A 50 entry return stack handles return predictions, just as on Oryon 1. However, testing shows that Oryon 3 can use all 50 entries before hitting a performance degradation. When call depth exceeds return stack capacity, Oryon 3 degrades gracefully rather than immediately taking a drastic penalty as Oryon 1 does. Oryon 1’s performance drop is heavy enough to suggest it’s mispredicting every return after the return stack overflows.
Perhaps Qualcomm implemented a new mechanism to keep a single overflow from messing up the entire return stack, and lets Oryon 3 only mispredict returns whose addresses get forced out on an overflow. Whatever this optimization is, it gives Oryon 3 return prediction behavior in-line with many other cores, including AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, AMD’s Zen 5 has a slightly larger 52 entry return stack.
Rename/Allocate Optimizations
Optimizations at the rename and allocate stage on Qualcomm’s big core are remarkably similar to those on its little core counterpart. Both cores can eliminate up to two register-to-register MOVs per cycle. They can also eliminate up to two add-immediate instructions, as long as their immediates sum to 255 or less. It’s slightly strange that Qualcomm has kept the same optimization capability even though the big core is more than twice as wide as its little core companion. That results in degraded microbenchmark figures when I chain dependent MOVs or add-immediate instructions without a break, because the wider core can get more of those instructions into the same rename group, which means the two-per-cycle restriction causes more missed optimization opportunities.
Backend: Large, and Largely Unchanged
One of the best strategies in CPU architecture is to avoid changing something that isn’t broken. Oryon 3’s backend at a high level is basically identical to the one in its predecessor. That makes sense because if Oryon 1 encountered performance issues, they likely had little to do with its backend strategy. Qualcomm specifies a reorder buffer capacity of over 650 micro-ops for both Oryon 1 and Oryon 3. Microbenchmarking puts capacity at 675 micro-ops for Oryon 3, and 680 on Oryon 1. Register files and memory ordering queues see little to no movement in size as well.
Qualcomm’s choice to avoid major backend changes is justified, because Oryon 3’s backend structures remain competitively sized even against emerging competition like AMD’s Zen 6. Execution throughput also remains competitive. Oryon 3 does have slightly smaller memory ordering queues, and weaker vector execution throughput compared to its x86-64 counterparts. The latter comes down to having a smaller 128-bit vector width, which is especially a disadvantage against Zen 5. However, that should only affect a small minority of applications.
Even though Oryon 3’s backend is similar to its predecessor, there’s still plenty of change under the hood. Predication is a central feature in SVE2 and SME, so Oryon 3 gets a new 120 entry predicate register file. The predicate registers themselves only have to be 16 bits wide because of Oryon 3’s 128-bit vector length. But while the predicate register file doesn’t need a lot of storage, it does need to be hooked up to every major execution unit block. Predicate generation can happen from both the scalar and vector side. All four vector pipes and four load/store pipes support predication, meaning a lot of reads from the predicate register file.
New SVE2 and SME instructions also require changes to backend logic. SVE’s vector length agnostic design rides heavily on predicate generation instructions like those of the WHILE* variety (like WHILELO). Oryon 3 breaks WHILE* instructions into two micro-ops, which execute through the integer pipes to deliver a throughput of one WHILE* instruction per cycle. Predicate generation instructions that don’t require a GPR input, like PTRUE and CMPEQ, execute through two FP/vector pipes. Besides predication focused changes, SVE2 adds new math instructions like CDOT, meaning more execution unit functionality behind the vector/FP ports.
Load/Store
Like Oryon 1, Oryon 3 has a four-pipe load/store unit. Memory dependencies are handled by a robust store forwarding mechanism, which can do fast forwarding for all cases where a load overlaps a prior store. Oryon 3 is able to do thai even when the load isn’t contained within the older store, meaning the load/store unit is able to combine data from both an in-flight store and data fetched from the L1 data cache. A dependent store+load pair has a latency of 6 cycles on the integer side, or 8 cycles on the vector/FP side. While Oryon 3 can’t do zero-latency store forwarding the way AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove can, the ability to avoid the 14 or 19 cycle penalty those cores take in partial overlap cases is quite nice. Arm’s Cortex X925 has the weakest store forwarding capabilities of the bunch, with no zero-cycle capability and a 12-13 cycle partial overlap penalty.
For independent accesses, Oryon 3 prefers 16B alignment for stores. Stores that cross a 16B boundary take a slight penalty, though curiously there’s no penalty for crossing a 64B cacheline boundary. Perhaps Oryon 3 has a special optimization for speeding up line-crossing stores. The same characteristics apply on the vector side.
SVE introduces scatter and gather functionality to the load/store unit, forcing it to handle possibly non-contiguous accesses from a single instruction. Testing with LD1W gathers (32-bit elements) achieves a core-wide throughput of 1-2 elements per cycle. Gathers therefore have lower throughput not just compared to contiguous loads, but also equivalent scalar loads. However, Oryon 3 has an optimization that allows repeated gather loads to the same address to execute at 4/cycle. Gathers therefore seem capable of using all four LSU pipes, and don’t go down a smaller subset of specialized pipes. However, the general case seems to rely on a complex flow that involves several micro-ops, resulting in lower throughput.
Dependent gathers have 14 cycle latency, which is acceptable for a non-contiguous load operation. Zen 5 handles vaguely equivalent AVX2 gathers with 19 cycle latency.
The load/store unit also has to translate program-visible virtual addresses to physical addresses that correspond to DRAM locations (or possibly MMIO). Qualcomm sized up the L1 DTLB from a 224 entry 7-way structure on Oryon 1, to a 256 entry 8-way one on Oryon 3. Perhaps Qualcomm always intended for the L1 DTLB to be 256 entries and 8-way set associative like the instruction-side L1 TLB, but couldn’t fit the last way into Oryon 1. A 256 entry L1 DTLB covers 1 MB of address space using 4 KB pages, which is a lot compared to the smaller L1 DTLBs on other designs. An 8K entry L2 TLB handles larger memory footprints, and serves both instruction and data accesses. The L2 TLB’s capacity is also impressive compared to the competition.
Comparing with Zen 5 can be complicated because AMD can opportunistically use a single TLB entry to cover up to four consecutive 4 KB pages, provided the translations have the same attributes and lead to contiguous physical pages. Zen 5 can cover more address space with its TLBs despite a lower entry count if it can make maximum use of that page coalescing capability, though I don’t have data on how effective that is in practice.
Testing with performance counters validates Qualcomm’s large TLB sizes. The core’s PMU indicates a rise in L1D TLB misses after 1 MB, when testing accesses with a 4 KB stride. L2 TLB misses rise after 32 MB, though they only sharply increase after 64 MB.
Qualcomm specifies 2-cycle latency for L2 TLB accesses, which would be incredible for a 8K entry L2 TLB. However, comparing L2 latency with 4 KB and 2 MB pages suggests that a L2 TLB hit costs at least an extra 6-7 cycles of latency.
Cache and Memory Access
Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite used a two-level caching strategy that emphasizes speed over the ability to scale last level cache capacity and the number of cores served by each last level cache instance. For the Snapdragon X2 Elite Qualcomm upgraded the cache subsystem by increasing L2 capacity from 12 to 16 MB for the P-Core clusters. This cache capacity increase boosts the amount of cache a single core can allocate into. It also helps account for each cluster having six cores instead of four, though cache per core still drops slightly from 3 MB on Oryon 1 to 2.66 MB in Oryon 3.
16 MB of CPU-side last level cache isn’t large by 2026 standards. AMD’s standard Zen 5 configurations use 32 MB of L3 cache, while Intel’s Arrow Lake has 36 MB of L3. However, Qualcomm’s caching capacity is fine next to the 16 MB of L3 that AMD puts in their mainstream Strix Point mobile chip’s performance cluster, and Qualcomm makes their L2 fast for the capacity it provides. With 20-23 cycle latency depending on which core is making the access, Qualcomm’s L2 can return data faster than the 46 cycle latency that AMD’s optimization guide specifies for Zen 5’s L3. AMD’s 46 cycle figure seems to apply to configurations with 32 MB of L3, like on the Ryzen 9 9900X. A Zen 5 variant with 96 MB of L3 incurs several extra cycles of latency, showing how a triple level cache subsystem can enable last level cache capacity scaling because the core-private L2 cache reduces sensitivity to L3 latency. Intel’s Lion Cove is Oryon 3’s opposite with respect to caching strategy, with four cache levels to enable capacity/speed tradeoffs at L2 and L3.
20+ cycles of L2 latency is still high compared to 14 cycles on AMD’s Zen 5, so Oryon 3 uses a large 96 KB 6-way L1D. Unusually for a high frequency design, Oryon 3 achieves 3 cycle L1D latency. It’s an impressive achievement, because even Arm’s lower clocked Cortex X925 has 4 cycle latency to a smaller 64 KB L1D.
Oryon 3 only shows a slight latency increase as a pointer chasing test spills out of the L1D when using a 64 byte stride. Using a shorter stride increases the length of the pointer chasing chain, and more clearly shows the L1D’s capacity. Qualcomm seems to have a “correlated miss caching” (CMC) style prefetcher like many of Arm’s designs, which tracks when a cache miss for one address is likely to be followed by a second miss to another address. This type of prefetcher can follow pointer chasing chains and defeat latency testing if the tested chain falls within what the prefetcher can remember. If Qualcomm is doing this, and they do suggest it by indicating they have “pointer” prefetching algorithms, then the data above points to it being a L1D prefetcher.
Arm in contrast places their CMC prefetcher at L2, which lets it be more aggressive because a larger L2 cache is less sensitive to having some capacity wasted by useless prefetches. For example, the CMC prefetcher on Arm’s Cortex A78 is able to reduce latency across the Mediatek Genio 1200’s 2 MB L3 when testing with a 64B stride compared to a 8B stride (at least 32K pointer destination predictions compared to 8K on Oryon 3).
Bandwidth
Oryon 3’s L1D can service four accesses per cycle, all four of which can be loads, and two of which can be stores. Compared to Zen 5 and Lion Cove, Oryon 3’s maximum load bandwidth is held back by its 128-bit vector width. However, Oryon 3 should remain very competitive when running code that can’t be well vectorized, or vectorized code that doesn’t scale to longer vector lengths.
L2 bandwidth is just under 32B/cycle for reads, in terms of how much data the core can get into registers. Qualcomm states that each core has a 64B/cycle datapath to L2. This can be validated by only accessing the first 128 bits of each 64B line, and treating that as loading the entire line because cache fills happen at 64B line granularity. Doing so gives about 48B/cycle of inferred L2 to L1D bandwidth. A read-modify-write pattern that creates equal traffic in both the L1D fill and writeback directions also reaches 48B/cycle.
I have a separate piece for more on the Snapdragon X2 Elite’s system level memory subsystem characteristics. Overall though, there’s a lot to like about Oryon 3’s memory subsystem. As long as you don’t benefit from having more than 16 MB of last level cache in each core cluster, Qualcomm’s cache setup should be more than a match for the triple level setups used by Intel, AMD, and other Arm cores.
Performance: SPEC CPU2026
Because running Linux on the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme is complicated at the moment and difficult considering other time constraints (Chips and Cheese isn’t a job after all, and I have a real job to pay attention to), I tested SPEC CPU2026 using Windows Subsystem on Linux. I’m pinning the vmmemWSL process to a P-Core for predictability. Results show the Oryon 3 P-Core delivering desktop-level SPEC CPU2026 integer scores, even though it’s implemented in a laptop. That’s an impressive showing because desktop chips enjoy advantages like higher cache capacity, lower DRAM latency, and higher clock speeds. A comparison against a typical AMD or Intel mobile part would almost certainly hand Oryon 3 a victory rather than a tie.
Qualcomm does score slightly behind Zen 5 in SPEC’s floating point suite, but manages to stay ahead of Intel. Individual subtests show modest differences between the cores, though there are outliers. 706.stockfish for example hands Zen 5 a large win, because GCC 14.2.0 was able to vectorize a large part of it to use AVX-512.
However, AVX-512 does not give AMD a huge lead in SPEC’s floating point workloads. 749.fotonik3d and 765.roms execute a lot of AVX-512 instructions on Zen 5, but Oryon 3 is able to compensate with higher IPC. Both workloads tend to be more memory bound as well, reducing the benefit of AMD’s higher vector throughput.
Further performance analysis is difficult without more work because WSL only passes through a subset of performance monitoring events. However, there’s enough data to show that Qualcomm’s branch prediction accuracy is up there with the best. Overall branch prediction accuracy is actually a bit better than that of AMD’s Zen 5. Oryon 3 even scores a win in 723.llvm, which is SPEC CPU2026’s toughest branch prediction workload.
Performance counters also show the merit of Oryon 3’s large L1D. L1D cache sizes have remained stubbornly stagnant outside of Qualcomm (and Apple) cores. In 1998, AMD rolled out their Athlon core with a 64 KB L1 data cache. No current cores from AMD, Intel, or Arm have a larger L1D, and I don’t put Lion Cove’s 192 KB “level 1 of the level 1 cache” in the same category as a conventional L1D because of its higher latency.
Each vendor’s performance monitoring unit accounts for L1D misses differently, but the differences are large enough to show that Qualcomm can service a lot more requests out of its fastest cache level than Intel or AMD.
Final Words
Third generation Oryon is a top-notch core with everything needed to succeed on a level playing field. Qualcomm has given their core a large out-of-order engine, is able to run it at 5 GHz, and feeds it with a competent branch predictor and a low latency cache setup. Oryon 3 joins Arm’s Cortex X925 in delivering desktop-level performance, and both Arm cores should be seen as serious pacing challenges for Intel and AMD.
Oryon 3 isn’t perfect of course. A wider SVE vector width could improve its situation relative to Zen 5 in vectorized workloads. Going to six vector/floating point pipes like in Arm’s Cortex X925 is an option too, though it may be difficult to pull off without regressing clock speeds. Qualcomm’s branch predictor could pick up some of the two taken branches per cycle goodness that’s now common on AMD, Arm, and Intel cores. Cache capacity could be an issue too, because a two-level cache setup forces a tightly coupled L2 design to meet latency requirements. That could make cache capacity difficult to scale.
All of those are areas for improvement, rather than significant weaknesses. SPEC scores for example show that a core doesn’t need to sustain two taken branches per cycle to be up there with the best, at least not in this generation. As for cache capacity, I can’t think of a consumer scenario where that makes a huge impact except for gaming. Games of course struggle with a binary translation issue, which is outside Qualcomm’s control.
Binary translation does bring up a problem for Oryon 3 though, because having a good core is only one piece of the puzzle. The software ecosystem that Qualcomm has to work with is a persistent sticking point, because while Windows on Arm has improved over the years, it’s still not as polished as a native x86-64 setup. Qualcomm has also struggled with Linux support. It’s a missed opportunity, because Linux is increasingly being seen as a strong alternative to Windows due to Windows 11’s misplaced priorities. Linux applications are also more likely to have aarch64 versions, minimising the importance of binary translation. Beyond the software ecosystem, Qualcomm’s laptop push faces headwinds because high DRAM costs push consumers to defer buying new devices. Laptops with soldered memory are especially vulnerable, because there’s no chance of buying a device with less memory with hopes of upgrading it later once prices drop. These challenges must be frustrating for hardware engineers who worked on Oryon 3, because they’ve built their most competitive CPU architecture yet, but need more puzzle pieces to fall into place.
I hope Qualcomm continues to run the marathon of breaking into the PC market, and the puzzle pieces line up soon to enable success. Oryon 3 is an excellent core. I’ve used the Zenbook A16 laptop sampled by Asus on a recent casual trip, and used it as a daily driver for a few weeks. The laptop is subjectively as fast as my desktop back at home, and shows just how far Qualcomm has gone. I want to see the people who worked on it rewarded for what they achieved. I also hope to see the Oryon line grow with future generations, and keep pushing the leading edge of single threaded performance.

articles.title: Collection of preserved UI style guides
articles.body:
Marcin Wichary
25 November 2026 / 69 style guides
UI style guides
This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.
- Amiga (Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.
-         
      Amiga User Interface Style Guide
- Android Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.
-         
      Android Design
-         
      Material Design v1
-         
      Material Design v2
-         
      Design for Android
- BlackBerry BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.
-         
      BlackBerry Wireless Handheld User Interface Style Guide
-         
      BlackBerry PlayBook Tablet UI Guidelines
-         
      BlackBerry Smartphones UI Guidelines
-         
      BlackBerry 10 UI Guidelines
- CDE Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.
-         
      OSF/Motif Style Guide
-         
      Common Desktop Environment: Style Guide and Certification Checklist
- CUA Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.
-         
        System Application Architecture: Common User Access
-         
        Object-Oriented Interface Design: IBM Common User Access Guidelines
- GEM/TOS Graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS.
-         
      GEM User Interface Guidelines
-         
      The documentation for TOS
- GNOME GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.
-         
      GNOME Human Interface Guidelines
-         
      GNOME Human Interface Guidelines
-         
      GNOME Human Interface Guidelines
- iOS and iPadOS iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Apple’s mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.
-         
      iPhone Human Interface GuidelinesCovers the skeuomorphic era of iOS 1–6
-         
      iOS Human Interface GuidelinesCovers iOS 7+
-         
      iPad Human Interface Guidelines
-         
      Apple Human Interface Guidelines
- Java Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.
-         
      Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines
-         
      Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines (2nd edition)
-         
      Java Look and Feel Design Guidelines: Advanced Topics
- Macintosh These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the “classic” Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.
-         
      Apple Lisa
-         
      Apple II
-         
      Human Interface Guidelines
-         
      Macintosh Human Interface Guidelines
-         
      Mac OS 8 Human Interface Guidelines
- Mac More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.
-         
      Aqua Human Interface GuidelinesCovers early years of Aqua
-         
      Apple Human Interface GuidelinesCovers evolving Aqua
-         
      OS X Interface GuidelinesCovers the era between pure Aqua and Liquid Glass
-         
      Apple Human Interface Guidelines
- Magic Cap An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.
-         
      Magic Cap Concepts
- Microsoft Office Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.
-         
      Microsoft Office System User Interface Design Guidelines
- NeXTSTEP NeXTSTEP was NeXT’s influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.
-         
        NeXTstep Concepts
-         
        NeXTSTEP User Interface Guidelines
-         
        OpenStep User Interface Guidelines
- Newton Apple Newton was Apple’s PDA launched in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.
-         
      Newton 2.0 User Interface Guidelines
- Nokia Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.
-         
    The User Interface of Nokia 9110 Communicator
-         
      S60 UI Style Guide
-         
      Symbian3 UI Style Guide
-         
      Symbian Belle UI Style Guide
- OPEN LOOK OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.
-         
      OPEN LOOK: Graphical User Interface Functional Specification
-         
      OPEN LOOK: Graphical User Interface Application Style Guidelines
- Palm OS Palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palm’s mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.
-         
        Palm OS User Interface Guidelines
-         
        Zen of Palm
- PenPoint PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.
-         
      PenPoint UI Design Guidelines
- RISC OS RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.
-         
      RISC OS Style Guide
- Samsung Various Samsung style guides.
-         
      The Samsung Gear UI Design Guidelines
-         
      One UI Design Guidelines
-         
      Samsung Smart TV Design Guides
- Silicon Graphics Style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.
-         
      SGI Indigo Magic User Interface Guidelines
-         
      SGI IRIX Interactive Desktop User Interface Guidelines
- Taligent Taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.
-         
      Human Interface Guidelines
- webOS webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.
-         
        Palm webOS User Interface Design Guidelines
-         
        Palm Design Guide
-         
        HP Touchpad webOS Design Guidelines
- Windows Does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.
-         
      Microsoft Windows Software Development Kit Application Style Guide
-         
      The Windows Interface: An Application Design Guide
-         
      The Windows Interface Guidelines for Software Design
-         
      Microsoft Windows User Experience: Official Guidelines for User Interface Developers and Designers
-         
      User Experience – Official Guidelines for User Interface Developers and Designers
-         
      Windows XP Visual Guidelines
-         
      Windows 8–10 User Experience Guidelines
-         
      Design basics for Windows apps
- Windows Phone Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6, and continuing through Windows Phone 7.
-         
      Designing Applications for Windows Mobile Powered Platforms
-         
      UI Design and Interaction Guide for Windows Phone 7
That’s it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.
Some of the above mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier – stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds.
You can also download all the above style guides in one archive.
Thank you to the following people for their collections that contributed to the above – you should check them out, since each one offers a different take and interface:
- Geof Crowl’s
- Matt Sephton’s (with help from Mario Guzmán and Brendan Donohoe)
- Matthias Rauterberg’s
- Přemysl Eric Janouch’s

articles.title: Defang Security Incident
articles.body:
On November 12, 2026 an attacker copied the credentials we use to run Defang and downloaded a copy of our main database. Here is what happened, what was exposed, what we have done, and what you should do.
On November 12, 2026 an attacker got into the Defang Deploy build system and copied the credentials we use to run Defang. With those they downloaded a copy of our main database. We confirmed this on November 23, 2026. If you have a Defang Portal account, your account is in that database, and this post explains what was taken and what you should do. We are also writing to every affected user by email.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, some of those credentials could also be used against your GitHub repositories and your cloud account. We have replaced them, but there are checks only you can do. They are listed under "What you should do" below. Please go through them as soon as you can.
What happened
We used a separate GitHub App for local development and testing. It was installed on two of our own repositories and had more permissions than it needed, including permission to change deployment environments. Acting as that app, the attacker pushed a commit to one of those repositories and tagged it as a release. Our production environment trusted release tags, so their code ran in our CI with access to our production credentials, and the attacker copied them.
The activity we can see ran from about 06:00 to 10:30 UTC on November 12. The credentials stayed valid until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12. Some of our logs are not detailed enough to rule that out, so we will update this post when we know more.
Timeline
All times are UTC.
- November 12, 06:05: the first workflow that copied build credentials ran, against our development and staging environments.
- November 12, 06:26: our production credentials were copied.
- November 12, 07:57 to 08:10: the database was copied.
- November 15: we were made aware of a security issue with a dependency and installed the update.
- November 23: a routine security scan found suspicious activity in our repositories.
- November 23: we confirmed the database copy from our access logs, replaced our production credentials and emailed every affected user.
- November 24: we published this post.
What the attacker could see
- Your name and email address. This is the address only: the attacker did not get into your email account or see any of your messages.
- Your GitHub or GitLab username, and the names of the organizations that account belongs to
- The answers you gave when you signed up
- If you installed the Defang GitHub App: the names of the repositories it can access, including private ones
- The cloud accounts you connected to Defang (account, project or subscription IDs and regions; no credentials)
- The Compose files you deployed or generated with Defang
- Copies of deployment state from deploys between October 12 and November 19. These can include database passwords and any environment variable built from a defang config value, such as a database URL that contains a password.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: what the attacker could use
The attacker could use the Defang GitHub App's key, and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. The token was stored encrypted, but the encryption key was taken too. Until we replaced them on November 23, anyone holding these could do in your repositories what the app is allowed to do:
- push commits and branches
- change workflow files and start workflow runs
- overwrite Actions secrets and variables
- change deployment environments and their protection rules
- open and merge pull requests
- change repository settings, including branch protection, deploy keys and collaborators
A workflow run started this way can receive your cloud credentials, because the role Defang set up for GitHub deploys trusts workflows in your repository.
If you have billing details with us
The copied credentials included a key for our account at Stripe, our payment provider. Until we replaced it on November 23, someone holding that key could read the record Stripe keeps for you:
- your name and email address
- your billing address, or the parts of it you gave us, and your tax ID if you entered one
- the brand, last four digits and expiry date of your card
- your subscription and invoice history
Your full card number and security code were not exposed. Stripe holds those and does not make them available to Defang or to anyone using our key.
What was not exposed
- Passwords. Defang has none for you: you sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code.
- Your cloud credentials. We never hold them. Your BYOC deployments run in your own account with your own credentials, and Defang's servers have no direct access to that account or to anything running in it. The one indirect path is the GitHub Actions deploy role described above.
- The contents of your repositories. They are not stored in our database.
- Config values you set with defang config. They stay in your cloud account, except for the copies in deployment state described above.
What we have done
- Replaced the Defang GitHub App key and secrets on November 23, and revoked the GitHub sign-in tokens we held.
- Replaced our other production credentials, including database, payment and email credentials, on November 23.
- Signed out every session and invalidated every Defang access token issued before November 23.
- Stopped keeping copies of deployment state on November 19 and deleted the copies we had.
- Cancelled every pending cloud invite link. If you were inviting someone, send a new invite.
- Notified GitHub, who are helping us audit for token misuse.
- Installed the security update on November 15.
- Revoked the development GitHub App's credentials and suspended the app on November 23.
- Reverted the production and staging deployment configurations that were altered by the attacker.
- Notified users and relevant authorities of the data breach.
What you should do
Everyone
- Be careful with email that claims to come from Defang, GitHub or GitLab, especially anything that asks you to sign in, approve an app or share a code. Someone holding this data can write a convincing message that uses your real name and username. We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- You will need to sign in to Defang again.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub
- Check your connected repositories for activity you don't recognize since November 11:
  - new commits, branches or tags
  - changes under .github/workflows
  - workflow runs you didn't start
  - changed Actions secrets or variables
  - new deploy keys or collaborators, and changed branch protection rules
- Look in particular at anything from defang-app[bot]. Your security log is at github.com/settings/security-log; organizations have an audit log under Settings.
- Lock down the deployment environments Defang created. In each connected repository, open Settings, then Environments. For every environment whose name starts with defang-, set "Deployment branches and tags" to your deploy branch only. You can also add required reviewers. This stops a workflow on any other branch from receiving your cloud credentials.
- Revoke and reconnect Defang's access to your GitHub account. In GitHub, go to Settings, then Applications, then Authorized GitHub Apps, and revoke Defang. Sign in to Defang again afterwards.
- If you no longer deploy from GitHub with Defang, uninstall the Defang app from your account or organization.
If you deploy from GitHub Actions: in your cloud account
- Check who has used your deploy role since November 11. The role or identity Defang set up for GitHub deploys has administrator access to your account. A token from a branch or workflow you don't deploy from is a sign of misuse.
  - On AWS this is usually defang-cd-CIRole. Search CloudTrail for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls on it.
  - On Google Cloud, check the workload identity pool's token exchanges.
  - On Azure, check the sign-in logs for the managed identity.
- Narrow that role's trust to the branch or environment you deploy from, if it currently allows any branch.
If you deployed with Defang between October 12 and November 19
- Change your database passwords and any secret that was part of another environment variable, then redeploy. Use defang config set <NAME> for each one.
- If your Compose file has secrets written directly in it, change those too.
If you have billing details with us
You do not need to replace your card. The exposed details are not enough to charge it. Watch your statements as you normally would, and be wary of email or calls that quote your last four digits or billing address to appear legitimate.
If any of these checks turns up something you don't recognize
Rotate the secrets in that repository's Actions secrets and environments and the cloud credentials its workflows can reach, then tell us.
Frequently asked questions
Was my GitHub password exposed? Do I need to change it right away?
No. Defang never had your GitHub password. You sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code, so there is no password for us to lose.
What the attacker could use was the Defang GitHub App's key and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. We replaced the key and revoked those tokens on November 23. Changing your GitHub password is not required, but it does no harm, and turning on two-factor authentication is a good idea in any case. The checks that matter are the ones under "If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub" above: look for activity you don't recognize, lock down deployment environments, and revoke the Defang GitHub App.
Did they take only my information from GitHub, or did they go further? Did they get my email?
They got your email address, but not your email account. The address we have on file for you is in our database, so it was copied. Defang has no access to your mailbox, so the attacker could not read your email or sign in to your email account through us.
From GitHub, what we hold is your username, the names of the organizations your account belongs to and, if you installed the Defang GitHub App, the names of the repositories it can access. The contents of your repositories are not in our database.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, the attacker also held the credentials that let them act in your repositories until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12, and we will update this post when we know more. That is why we ask you to review your repositories and your cloud account. "What the attacker could see" and "What the attacker could use" above list everything.
Did this happen only to me, or to all users?
Anyone with a Defang Portal account is in the database that was copied, so your email address, and potentially your name, was exposed along with everyone else's. Beyond that, what was exposed depends on how you use Defang. See above section for details.
How can I protect my data? How do I check that an email really comes from you?
- Don't sign in, approve an app or share a code because an email asked you to. Open the Defang Portal, GitHub or GitLab yourself by typing the address in your browser, rather than following a link in a message.
- We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- Someone holding this data can quote your real name, username or the organizations you belong to. A message that knows those details is not proof that it comes from us.
- If you are unsure about a message, forward it to sec@defang.io and we will tell you whether we sent it.
- Work through the checklist in "What you should do" above. In short: review your repositories, review your cloud account, change database passwords and secrets if you deployed between October 12 and November 19, and turn on two-factor authentication on your GitHub and cloud accounts.
How do I delete my account and data?
Open Settings in the Defang Portal and delete your account there, or email sec@defang.io and we will do it for you.
Contact us
If you find anything suspicious, or want an engineer to go through your account, repositories or cloud account with you, write to sec@defang.io. We will update this post as we learn more.
The Defang Team

On November 12, 2026 an attacker copied the credentials we use to run Defang and downloaded a copy of our main database. Here is what happened, what was exposed, what we have done, and what you should do.

We are also writing to every affected user by email.

We used a separate GitHub App for local development and testing. Our production environment trusted release tags, so their code ran in our CI with access to our production credentials, and the attacker copied them.
The activity we can see ran from about 06:00 to 10:30 UTC on November 12. The credentials stayed valid until we replaced them on November 23. - your billing address, or the parts of it you gave us, and your tax ID if you entered one

articles.title: The Verge’s guide to affordable holiday gifts under $25
articles.body:
Gift-giving on a tight budget is tough, but constraints can also encourage some creative thinking. We thought for a long while (and asked other Verge staffers) about the best items out there, and we’re pretty happy with what we came up with.
The Verge’s guide to affordable holiday gifts under $25
Whether it’s stocking stuffers or a little treat for yourself, these are some of our favorite gifts under $25.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
For this list, we’ve rounded up a barrage of fun gadgets and stocking-stuffer specials. You’ll find nostalgic ways to spruce up a room like Play-Doh’s Blooms, fancy ways to jot down notes like the Pilot Kakuno fountain pen, and plenty of tech-forward extras like the Time Timer Mod. It’s time to get creative with your budget buys, and this list can get you there.
Lamicall magnetic cord organizers
Lamicall’s magnetic cord organizers are simple yet effective tools. They hold the ends of your most frequently used cables so they don’t fall to the floor when you unplug them, and the low-cost accessories can be stuck to the side of your desk or kitchen counter. They also work great behind your entertainment center or wherever else is convenient.
Play-Doh Blooms
There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.
Time Timer Mod (Home Edition)
For visual learners, a visible timeline can help keep the pace moving. The Time Timer Mod provides an aesthetically pleasing 60-minute countdown to help your favorite procrastinator stay on task and maximize efficiency, no matter what they’re working on.
TP-Link Kasa smart plug three-pack
Smart plugs are the easiest way to bring older electronics into the 21st century. For the smart home fan in your life, TP-Link’s Kasa plugs are a brilliant budget-friendly buy, adding Google or Amazon Alexa voice assistance to everyday items, not to mention power schedules and remote control. Note: They support 2.4GHz Wi-Fi connectivity only.
For the giftee who likes to keep things on the level (literally), this striking 12-inch leveling tool offers the traditional bubble measure alongside LED lights that turn from red when the level needs adjusting to green when it locks in. It’s just a slightly more satisfying way to ensure you’re level before drilling or hammering.
Aothia desk mat
Sometimes a little change can make a big difference. Aothia’s desk mats bring aesthetic and functional improvements in an array of stylish color options, with a smooth faux leather surface that protects your desktop and can bring some much-needed order to your desk layout.
These magnetic word tiles are a classic for a reason. Sure, silly phrases or profound thoughts on a fridge door won’t change the world, but they could brighten a housemate’s day. If anything, slowing down a few times a day to read these fun messages as you open the fridge is a welcome break that we all could use.
If you’ve got a scribe on your list who prefers the feel of paper instead of digital screens, give their pencils or fountain pens something to dig into with the Midori MD Note pad. Cream-colored paper, wide lines, and 185-degree binding combine for a great way to jot down anything that comes to mind.
These dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connection, simple setup, and Matter compatibility so they can seamlessly fit into Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home smart home systems. Best of all, these smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.
These Ikea pegboards are a great gift for anyone looking to organize a bedroom, office, or dorm room. They’re available in multiple sizes and colors, and they can be presented in your space in multiple ways, be it mounted on the wall or stood on a desk. Extra accessories make it even easier to organize doodads.
The comedy streaming service created by CollegeHumor alumni offers endless, ad-free entertainment for the improv lover in your life. With multiple shows from some of the top names in comedy, and a business model that encourages profit sharing for creators, it’s a feel-good way to bring more laughter to someone’s life.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.
This moldable material is more than just glue. It’s useful for practical tasks, like fixing drywall, crafting your own cable management system, or just to build for fun. Sugru glue comes in multiple colors and serves as a smart solution to any number of household problems, especially for people who don’t have access to a 3D printer.
Ynesoer automatic soap dispenser
This once-futuristic automatic soap dispenser has become affordable enough for anyone to own. This particular model is one that a Verge staffer owns and likes, thanks to its customizable portions for the perfect hands-free wash. It’s especially great if you cook a lot and don’t want to touch your soap dispenser.
Maxracy garlic roller
For the chef on your list, these convenient garlic peelers make it easy to strip off the skin without crushing the cloves. In other words, it does the most annoying part of dealing with garlic on your behalf. If only it were this easy to tell them they need to take the garlic down a notch in their red sauce.
This truncated version of the popular Wingspan card game offers an easier point of entry in terms of cost and complexity. Players act as bird enthusiasts collecting various types of birds through multiple rounds for their wildlife preserve. Designed for one to five players, each game takes around 30 minutes or less.
These aren’t your grandma’s measuring spoons. Unless, of course, your grandma is super hip and fun, in which case they’re an excellent gift for her, or... she may already have them. With snazzy designs in vivid colors, these silly spoons spice things up in more ways than one.
For those who aspire to use something better than the plain Bic or Paper Mate pen, this affordable fountain pen is great for the aspiring calligrapher on your list. Its design is light and ergonomic, and it includes a single ink cartridge to get them started. This could be the start of a really fun hobby.
Gear Aid Heroclip
Anyone looking for a good stocking stuffer should grab this handy carabiner-style clip. While not everyone will have a use for one, you’ll probably know who on your list will dig its aircraft-grade aluminum frame that supports up to 50 pounds. It even swivels to double as a hanger in a pinch.
Show your support for our journalism while also sprucing up that coffee mug cabinet with a fresh addition. These Verge-branded 15-ounce mugs offer minimalist style and plenty of space for that extra pour you’ll need to make it through the workday, until daycare pickup, or during a long and lazy Sunday.
Sometimes, a straight, regular USB-C cable just won’t suffice. This cable is a fantastic choice for two reasons: First, it’s coiled, letting it expand from around 1 foot to 5 feet; and second, the right-angle connector makes it easier to plug into some difficult-to-reach ports instead of bending.
Get your favorite Pokémon lover a fun piece of merchandise they can piece together. With one of 15 different models (including Slowpoke, our favorite), this model kit includes four different eye sticker options, and at about 4.5 inches long, it fits neatly on a desk, a side table, or on a curio shelf next to other beloved tchotchkes.
Magnetic drawing board for toddler
Finding it hard to shop for that young niece or nephew? We’ve got you covered with this fun and colorful magnetic drawing board, which can be used to focus their creative energy. And maybe, just maybe, it’ll keep them from turning loose on the living room wall with a Sharpie set or crayons.
In the days before Bombas, socks used to be a lame gift. Now, gifting the right pair can make you the hero, especially if you choose pairs like these merino wool socks, which are machine-washable and designed to keep the chill at bay during those cold winter months as well as brisk nights and mornings.

articles.title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
articles.body:
Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.
Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.
“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.
In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.
