articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: 1Password Security Incident
articles.body:
Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
by 1Password
November 25, 2026 - 4 min
Related Categories
What happened
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.
What information was affected
The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:
- Names and email addresses
- Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
- Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
- Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
- Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
- Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.
When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
What was not affected
- Your vaults and the items in them
- The keys that protect your vaults 
  - 1Password does not store your account password or secret key
- Account recovery keys
- 1Password apps and browser extensions
What we’ve done
- Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
- Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
- Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
- Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
- Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
- Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
- Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
- 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
- Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
- If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

articles.title: Why Automated Proof-Solving Is the Same Old Dead End
articles.body:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026]
Title:The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.
The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

articles.title: Invisible Wave Hits California, Oregon and Canada as Towns Evacuate
articles.body:
On Monday, seawater was already flooding buildings in a small Northern California fishing community, and the worst of this week’s tides had not yet arrived. By Tuesday morning, residents of King Salmon on Humboldt Bay had been ordered to leave. The Humboldt County Sheriff’s Office warned that water levels could climb toward 10 feet if the current tidal anomaly persists, close to the bay’s all-time record of 10.37 feet. Forecasters say sustained southerly winds this week will push the storm surge even higher. Humboldt Bay is only the leading edge of a coastal flood threat that stretches more than 1,000 miles, from Southern California to British Columbia, and it is being driven by a wave almost nobody can see.
That wave is a Kelvin wave, a vast pulse of warm water sent east across the equatorial Pacific by the fast-strengthening El Niño. It does not break on the beach or arrive as a wall of water. It raises the baseline height of the ocean itself, lifting the sea surface along the coast and holding it there for weeks or even months. Forecasters estimate it has raised sea levels off Southern California by 5 to 8 inches, and some projections put the rise at a full foot. On an ordinary day that extra water would barely register, but this week the ocean is starting from a much higher point than usual.
The raised ocean has now arrived at the same time as the king tides, the highest astronomical tides of the year, which happen when the pull of the Moon and Sun line up. This set falls around a full Moon sitting close to perigee, the point in its orbit nearest to Earth, and forecasters say the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle is adding to the push. On top of that, a train of Pacific storms is bringing strong onshore winds, heavy rain and big surf. Each of these things can flood a coastline by itself, and this week all of them are happening together. Forecasters across the region have marked Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day as the most dangerous window.
In San Francisco, the National Weather Service has a coastal flood warning in force through Thursday afternoon, with the highest water expected around 11 a.m. on Wednesday. Forecasters expect the tide to reach about 2.8 feet above normal, almost level with the city’s record of 2.9 feet set during the storms of January 1983. On the Crissy Field gauge, that record reads 8.66 feet, and Wednesday’s official forecast stands at 8.6 feet, less than an inch below it. City officials are preparing for water above 9 feet in case the storm surge comes in stronger than expected.
Mayor Daniel Lurie has called the situation “extremely serious” and urged people to stay off flooded roads and avoid trips that are not essential, though he later said the forecast had improved somewhat. The weather service has flagged extreme flood risk along the bay shoreline, including around San Francisco International Airport and Oakland’s airport. Crews have put up a Tiger Dam barrier system near the Bay Bridge toll plaza, and the state closed the Posey Tube between Alameda and Oakland from Sunday night. On the open coast, breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet are forecast for Wednesday. The Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded in heavy rain only last week, is in the danger zone again.
The bay’s shape spreads the threat well beyond the Golden Gate. Water that enters from the Pacific moves through a large network of bays, sloughs and wetlands, reaching shorelines many miles from the open ocean. Marin County has told residents to take extra care between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. from Tuesday through Thanksgiving. On the Tiburon Peninsula, people in low-lying homes have been urged to think about leaving before each day’s highest tide. Around 1.5 inches of rain is forecast over two days, on top of the 3.2 inches that fell last week, so drains that normally empty into the bay may have nowhere for the water to go.
Southern California has already had a preview. On October 27, king tides arriving with the first push of the Kelvin wave set record high water levels at Santa Barbara, San Pedro, San Diego and La Jolla. In Huntington Beach alone, 114 structures were damaged, and floodwater reached Newport Beach, Long Beach, Redondo Beach and San Diego’s Mission Beach. One Mission Beach resident who had lived there for 30 years said he had never seen flooding like it. Forecasters expect some of those records to fall again this week, less than a month after they were set.
A coastal flood warning covers the whole Orange County coast until Friday, and forecasters say maximum sea levels could top 8 feet from Tuesday through Thursday. Some forecasts suggest Southern California tides could reach 9 feet or more, about a foot higher than October’s record. The weather service office in Oxnard has high confidence in record tides for Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties. Orange and San Diego counties are under extreme coastal flooding and high surf warnings for Thanksgiving Day, with major impacts also possible on Tuesday, Wednesday and Black Friday.
Coastal towns are building defenses as fast as they can. Newport Beach has built or reinforced about 5.3 miles of sand berms, handed out 150,000 sandbags and raised 70 public seawalls. In Huntington Beach, a 3.7-mile stretch of Pacific Coast Highway between Seal Beach Boulevard and Warner Avenue is closed, and low-lying roads are shut from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. every day this week. Crews in Huntington Harbour are wrapping seawalls in layers of sealed sandbags, and boaters have been told to stay away at high tide because their wakes can push water over the walls. On Dana Point’s Beach Road, ten homes have already been red-tagged and three destroyed, and owners are stacking boulders in front of what is left.
The heat in the water is part of the reason the ocean sits so high. NOAA data from November 12 to 18 showed a wide band of coastal water more than 10°F warmer than the 1971 to 2000 average. Warm seawater expands and takes up more room, which lifts the surface further. Off San Francisco, the sea has also been rising slowly for decades, by about 2 millimeters a year, which means every king tide starts a little higher than the last.
The threat continues north into Oregon and Washington, where weather service offices in Portland and Seattle have warned of coastal flooding through Friday. The worst is expected from Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day, when several weather systems bring strong winds and rising surf during high tide. Forecasters warn that waves could knock people off their feet or sweep them off rocks and into the ocean. Washington State Ferries has already cancelled several sailings because of the high tides, with around 300,000 people expected to use the ferry system over the holiday weekend. Heavy snow in the mountains could also slow travel over the passes, especially on Interstate 90 east of Seattle.
Across the border, Environment Canada says a series of deep low-pressure systems will cross the offshore waters this week, driving storm surge and large waves into the British Columbia coast. Combined with the king tides, these could push water 20 to 50 centimeters (about 8 to 20 inches) above the highest astronomical tide. Water levels are forecast to rise each day and peak on Thursday. Some areas could see 100 to 200 millimeters of rain, the B.C. River Forecast Centre has issued a high streamflow advisory for most of Vancouver Island, and an evacuation alert is in place for some shoreline properties of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation.
Boundary Bay is one of the spots being watched most closely. The bay is wide, shallow and low-lying, and it straddles the border between Delta, British Columbia, and Point Roberts, Washington. The City of Delta has warned that high water could hit Beach Grove, Boundary Bay and Westham Island from Tuesday, with the warning in effect until December 4. The city has put flood protection at beach access points and left sand and sandbags at Seaview Road, the 1A boat launch and the 3rd and 16th Avenue beach accesses.
This week is unlikely to be the end of it. A Kelvin wave can keep the coast raised long after the storms that rode on top of it have passed, and El Niño events usually send five or six of these waves across the Pacific. The 2015 to 2016 super El Niño produced five, and this one is strengthening faster and could become the strongest on record. The next round of king tides is due from December 22 to 26, around Christmas, with more in January, and forecasters say the higher ocean could last into early spring 2027. For towns from San Diego to Vancouver Island, the high water in the coming days may be the first of several rounds this winter.

articles.title: At Least You’ll Have Equity
articles.body:
I’ve been dipping my toe in the interview process after a year+ on the Pro Leisure Circuit. One of the more recent interviews was with a hardware company out of LA. When we first started chatting, I explained, “I’m a consumer software guy who has been hardware adjacent.”
Their response: “Don’t worry, we have plans; you’d be a great fit.”
Interviews. Then more interviews. I’m intrigued, but not sold.
The robots are excellent at research, so I researched. Interviews, podcasts, press releases, LinkedIn profiles. They wouldn’t tell me why I was a great fit, so I’d use the robots to figure it out. Several hours later, I jokingly realized why they wanted me. I typed this realization into Claude not because I was expecting a response, but… because.
“They want me to build Skynet.”
To which Claude immediately responded, “At least when it achieves consciousness, you’ll have equity.”
R.I.P. that opportunity.

articles.title: World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time
articles.body:
World Has Six Consecutive Days 2C Above Preindustrial Levels For First Time (theguardian.com) 6
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. "The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we'd been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C."
Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, said: "Another day, another global temperature record," adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been "smashed."

articles.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
articles.body:
FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue? (cnn.com) 41
			
		 	
				CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S..  A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit."
Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications.  They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure...
This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network...  On the day of the network meltdown, L3Harris was undertaking a maintenance job that involved switching the system from a decades-old router to a new one. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees.  Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process.  
The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. Previously, local technical operations managers, site technicians and others would determine when the work could be done with the least impact on air traffic and to game out worst-case scenarios. The union contends that process did not happen before L3Harris arrived at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site on November 13...  [David Spero, president of the union], contends the FAA has given private companies "too much authority and generally unfettered access." 
CNN also points out a 2009 incident where 129 of America's air traffic facilities experienced an outage of FAA telecommunications "that delayed thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide. 
"The cause: A technician with Harris Corp., which later merged with L3 Technologies to form L3Harris, incorrectly configured an FAA telecommunications router at the Los Angeles Center..."

articles.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
articles.body:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”
In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

articles.title: Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island
articles.body:
For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*
* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.
Getting a Payphone to a small island in the South Pacific
Step 1 was getting a payphone.
Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.
The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium. Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.
Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.
Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.
Programming
Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager, which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.
Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.
The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.
I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.
After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.
We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.
We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.
Talking to Santa
Once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.
We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.
The ATA the payphone is connected to just comes through to our IMS like any other fixed line subscriber; the TAS is setup to zero-rate the destination and then it’s dialplan forwards it to “Santa Bridge” listening for SIP on port 5090.
I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.
One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop, while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.
All the code for this is on Github.
Branding
The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a new one, with a retro style I really like.
Installation
The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.
He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.
Getting it on Payphone Tag
The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture.
Future payphone adventures
So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.
We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.
If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

articles.title: Slow Ubuntu security response times
articles.body:
Message-ID: <20261125172638.73c0a05b@hboeck.de>
Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:26:38 +0100
From: Hanno Böck <hanno@...eck.de>
To: oss-security@...ts.openwall.com
Subject: Slow Ubuntu security response times
Hello,
Lately, I'm observing that Ubuntu's response to severe security flaws
is concerning.
On November 16th, details about a remote memory corruption called
NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) in the Linux kernel's TCP stack were
published: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/15/2
Today, nine days later, Ubuntu still has not published a fix yet:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99288
Other distros had a fix already available when the details were
published.
Likewise, a KVM host escape (CVE-2026-99312) affecting AMD
virtualization published on Nov 18th has no fix yet either [3]:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99312
Ubuntu has been slow in patching another remote TCP corruption
(CVE-2026-98432) lately, where it took multiple weeks until a fix was
available. See also: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu
Recent news indicates that this is might be exploited in the wild:
https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign
I think everyone understands that these times aren't easy for security
teams. Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux
kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available
within hours, not days or weeks.
On a recent Ubuntu LTS system, the kernel version is 7.0.0-44. This
seems to indicate that Ubuntu is not relying on longterm supported
kernels from kernel.org, but is instead backporting patches to an old
kernel version. On a Debian stable system, the kernel version is
6.12.118+deb13, indicating that it's based on a very recent longterm
kernel from kernel.org. I would consider the backporting strategy for
the kernel to be hardly viable and probably everyone should base their
Linux kernels on longterm releases supported by the Linux kernel
developers.
-- 
Hanno Böck - Independent security researcher
https://itsec.hboeck.de/
https://badkeys.info/

articles.title: Holy Shit Holy Shit Holy Shit Holy Shit [Algorithmic Complexity Lower Bounds]
articles.body:
HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.
Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.
There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.
Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that!
But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)1/2+o(1). The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!). All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.
To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE—that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.
It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.
All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.
I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.
For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean certificates, don’t be a raging doofus who seizes on some triviality (e.g., a minor discrepancy between the Lean and informal proofs, or unused sections of the Lean proof) to pretend that dozens of great open problems of math and theoretical computer science are not, in fact, getting solved. Because they are getting solved. It might take us years to understand the solutions, but my working assumption by this point is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary.
I can’t possibly put the matter better than one of my friends on Facebook:
After years of crackpot “solutions” claiming Millennium Problems are solved, now that we have actual solutions, we have crackpot “refutations” claiming Millennium Problems are not solved. It is really poetic, in a way.
Along the way to so many lower bounds that we wondered whether ever we’d live to see, there will also, of course, be further shocking upper bounds: that is, ultimate barriers to lower bounds, also known as “algorithms.” And yes, some of those algorithms will break currently deployed cryptosystems.
Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area. However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells. I do not wish to be responsible for spreading unverified rumors. And I worry that exact statements of what was done may have been mangled in a game of Telephone.
I also, crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening. If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever. I don’t have what you’re looking for here.
Let me be clear: for those of my readers who celebrate, I believe that tomorrow would be a superb Thanksgiving to spend some quality time with your kids and parents and siblings and old friends.
Right now—this past week—is very much like I would’ve always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like. I just hope we’ll get lucky, and it will “merely” be a singularity for our little corner of the world that involves hard math problems.
At some point at dinner last night, Dana had a sneezing fit. So I said to her, I hope it isn’t a swarm of nanobots that’s come to infect us! But if it is, then I hope it’s the friendly kind, the kind that will usher us all into an AI utopia.
Now, of course, another morning has dawned, and we’re still here. May we find a world where we and our children will be happy to live at the bottom of this rollercoaster. May we work to make it so.

articles.title: Hazel (YC W24) Is Hiring a Product Designer
articles.body:
AI-enabled procurement for government
Our mission at Hazel is simple and powerful. We use AI to help U.S. government purchasing teams buy at the speed of need with unparalleled efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is a $2.7T problem every single year, and Hazel is at the forefront with Federal and State, Local, and Education (SLED) agencies.
Hazel has identified a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to solve this by deploying cutting-edge AI to the public sector and unlocking the full potential of our nation. We empower our partners to move with expediency against the most pressing challenges of this century. Hazel builds AI for the public interest.
Hazel is transforming government procurement: how government agencies purchase goods and services from commercial vendors. Our federal partners use our AI-forward bid evaluations solution to assess vendors more accurately, reliably, and quickly. With the federal government under increasing pressure to accelerate acquisitions, our tools give them a real edge.
Our COTS products, led by Document Builder and Evaluations, serve state & local governments, schools, and special authorities. The users are procurement officers working through long, high-stakes documents and decisions, and they deserve software that is as clear and trustworthy as it is powerful.
As Hazel's contract Product Designer, you will elevate the user experience and visual design of products government teams rely on daily. Hazel has built a substantial product based on deep understanding of our users' needs. In this role, you will refine our UI/UX and establish standards for our engineering team going forward.
There are three main deliverables:
Federal. Upgrade the UI/UX of the bid evaluations solution we are deploying for our largest federal contract.
Commercial. Improve the UX of our COTS product flows and define consistent UI elements to unify the product design.
Playbook. Deliver a practical style guide and Figma component set so Hazel engineers can ship consistent, high-quality UI after the engagement ends.
Audit Hazel's existing workflows and identify the highest-impact UI/UX improvements
Design high-fidelity screens, flows, and interaction states for complex, document-heavy workflows, including how users review and act on AI output
Work directly with Hazel's founders and engineers, sharing work early and iterating quickly
Hand off production-ready designs and review what ships to ensure quality
Build a reusable set of Figma components and documented patterns
Write a practical style guide our engineers can follow for new features, including accessibility basics (Section 508 / WCAG 2.1 AA)
Proven experience as a product designer or similar role, with a portfolio of shipped work
Strong skills across UI/UX
Experience designing complex, workflow-heavy B2B applications (dense tables, long forms, multi-step reviews and approvals)
Experience working within and contributing to a design system
Ability to improve an existing product without starting from scratch
Fast turnaround and independence: you ship in days, not weeks
Expert in Figma or similar tools
Excitement about bringing innovation to the public sector
Has worked at a startup or startup-like environment
Building a design system from scratch and documenting it for others
Front-end coding experience (React, TypeScript)
Designing AI features, including surfacing sources and letting users review and correct model output
Document-centric interfaces: reading, annotating, or comparing long documents
Working with or adjacent to the public sector
Accessibility work to Section 508 or WCAG 2.1 AA
Federal acquisition or source selection
$10,000 - $20,000/month depending on experience | Contract for 3-6 months, 20-40 hrs/week
Remote, with potential working sessions in person with the team. All travel expenses will be paid.
U.S. Citizenship required
Opportunity for future projects or a longer-term role
You will set the design standard for Hazel. Your work will ship to federal evaluators and to procurement teams across states, cities, and schools. The style guide you leave behind will shape every feature we build after.
You'll work side-by-side with inquisitive and driven founders as well as a world-class and dynamic founding engineering team, with frontline exposure to our government partners.
Hazel is a mission-driven organization founded by engineers and built around delivering world-class innovation to our government partners. We strive for excellence, deliver impact, and have fun doing it.
You care about mission. Hazel partners with agencies supporting everything from public school teachers in the classroom to warfighters in the field. We believe in products which change America for the better.
You want a startup that is structured without being rigid, quality-obsessed without being slow, and product-led without losing the vision. You take ownership: shaping the experience, talking to customers, and wearing many hats.
You solve problems. There's no more time to opine on strategy and policy when our nation faces existential challenges, today. We are workhorses, not showhorses.
You are always learning. Nobody has all the answers, and the world is ever-evolving, so we must be adaptive. We bring the best practices available from all domains to meet the challenge.
You believe in team. Our team grows together, supports one another, and elevates our shared successes. We are more effective together.
Our mission at Hazel is simple and powerful. We use AI to help U.S. government purchasing teams buy at the speed of need with unparalleled efficiency and cost-effectiveness. It is a $2.7T problem every single year, and Hazel is at the forefront with State, Local, and EDucation (SLED) and federal government agencies.
Government procurement has moved at a glacial pace for decades, stovepiped by complex processes, regulatory capture, and overworked civil servants. The impacts are severe. Our founders saw at Palantir and BCG how lowly procurement challenges fueled wildfires across California, compromised critical U.S. national security systems, and wasted billions of dollars.
Hazel has identified a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to solve this by deploying cutting-edge AI to the public sector and unlocking the full potential of our nation. We empower our partners to move with expediency against the most pressing challenges of this century including climate sustainability, great power competition, and more. Hazel builds AI for the public interest. The founders August and Elton saw this problem firsthand at Palantir and BCG, and they have enlisted a deep bench of investors from both tech and government to deploy one of the first real commercial applications of generative AI in the public sector.

articles.title: Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire
articles.body:
Windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll. It evens out the volume of each application, so quiet and loud parts play at a similar level.
- modules/loudness/: the PipeWire module and the DSP plugin. It processes every app's playback stream.
- modules/limiter/: the output limiter of Windows' audio engine (AudioEng.dll), on every playback device. It keeps the boost from clipping.
- app/: an optional window (GTK3) to turn it on or off, globally or per app, and set the release time.
Requires PipeWire ≥ 1.4, and GTK 3 for the window.
# Arch:   sudo pacman -S pipewire gtk3 pkgconf make gcc
# Debian: sudo apt install libpipewire-0.3-dev libspa-0.2-dev libgtk-3-dev pkg-config make gcc
make
sudo make install
systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber
To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness, make -C modules/limiter or make -C app. To uninstall, run sudo make uninstall and restart the same services.
Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq.
The settings live in a PipeWire metadata object, so they can also be scripted:
pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 enabled false                               # turn off
pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 release 6                                   # release time, 2 (fast) to 7 (slow)
pw-metadata -n loudness-eq 0 disabled-apps '["Discord"]' Spa:String:JSON  # leave these apps alone
pw-metadata -n loudness-eq                                               # show settings
Changes apply immediately and are kept across restarts.
Defaults are in /usr/share/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/60-loudness-eq.conf. To override them, copy it to ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/.
Settings changed at runtime are saved in ~/.local/state/pw-loudness-eq/state.conf and take precedence over this file.
The loudness module sets audioconvert.filter-graph.90 on each app's playback stream, so the plugin runs inside that stream, before its volume and before mixing, like a Windows stream effect.
The limiter module does what Windows' audio engine does on every playback device: after the mix and the software volume, it runs the output through a look-ahead limiter. It's always on, independent of Loudness Equalization, as on Windows.
Not processed: JACK clients, streams with more than 8 channels, and Flatpak apps that use PipeWire directly (those going through PulseAudio are processed).
A broadband automatic gain control. Despite the name, it doesn't equalize the spectrum.
- Frame size N = 2^⌈log2(fs/100)⌉ (512 at 44.1/48 kHz), with 50% overlap.
- Each channel is windowed with w[n] = 16384·(1 − cos(2π(n+½)/N)) / (N/2) and run through a real FFT to get the power spectrum.
- Power is summed into 25 bands with edges at 100, 200, 300, 400, 510, 630, 770, 920, 1080, 1270, 1480, 1720, 2000, 2320, 2700, 3150, 3700, 4400, 5300, 6400, 7700, 9500, 12000, 15500 and 24000 Hz. Channels are summed together.
- Loudness L = 1.72 · Σ max(E_b − T_b, 1e-32)^0.25, with T = 1000, 100, 31.6, 10, 3.16, 2, 1, 1, .316, .316, 1×11, 4, 10, 100, 1000.
- Target gain = min((1300/L)^1.6, 10), so at most +20 dB.
- When the target is lower than the current gain, the gain jumps to it instantly. Otherwise it moves toward it by w = (N/128)·(44100/fs)·0.1^min(r,3)·0.316^(min(r,7)−min(r,3)) per block. At r = 4 that's a time constant of about 4.6 s.
- The gain is crossfaded linearly across each half-frame. Latency is N samples.
The boost can push pure tones such as a whistle well above full scale; the limiter catches that.
Ported from CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dll. audiodg.exe puts it on every render device, after its effects, before the device.
- The output is delayed by L frames (64 at 44.1/48 kHz; 16, 32 or 128 at other rates) to look ahead. That's the device's added latency.
- When a frame entering the delay peaks above the tracked peak (initially 0.985), the gain ramps down linearly over those L frames to 0.985 / peak, reaching it as that frame leaves. All channels share one gain.
- The gain only recovers once the signal peaks at half the tracked peak or less: it rises by e^(2.205/fs) per frame (about 19 dB/s) while the tracked peak decays by the same factor.
On Windows the device's software volume comes before the limiter; in PipeWire it comes after the device's filter graphs. So the plugin gets the volume of each channel (kept in sync by the module), measures peaks on the signal as it will be after the volume, and applies only its gain. Once PipeWire applies the volume, the result is the same as Windows'. Hardware volume comes after the limiter on both.
make check                                              # DSP and plugin tests, both modules
modules/loudness/build/leq-wav [-r release] in.wav out.wav       # process a file offline

articles.title: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
articles.body:
This month’s Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual “Code Red” internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.
Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
In a memo to the teams responsible for Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson revealed the outage was the most significant in history for Microsoft’s customers. “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” said Henderson. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”
As part of this Code Red declaration, Microsoft is focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft now has a target of resolving future outages within an hour, and will reportedly deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose issues. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews.
In a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants.
Microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

articles.title: Smart People Who Give a Shit Use Tools
articles.body:
Anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.
Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.
The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.
I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.
Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.
When you hand a capable model to that engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.
The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.
Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve written before about the specific sinking feeling of staring at 800 lines of generated code you have no mental model of and deploying it with crossed fingers.
There’s a subtler hazard too, especially for people early in their careers: if you never wrestle with a weird bug or read a stack trace yourself, you never build the scar tissue that tells you when something smells wrong. And LLMs make laziness unusually tempting because of how they fail. A compiler yells at you loudly when you screw up; a model fails in smooth, confident prose that looks totally reasonable until production catches fire. That’s a genuine risk, and pretending it isn’t would be silly.
Still, look closely at what’s actually broken in that scenario. The trouble comes from shipping code nobody verified, without building a mental model, in an organization where nobody feels on the hook when it breaks. We had that exact engineer long before ChatGPT showed up. Ten years ago they pasted the top Stack Overflow answer without reading the comments, pulled in a bloated dependency to avoid thinking for twenty minutes, and stamped “LGTM” on every review after thirty seconds. Now they can coast as a human clipboard for a model, at least for a while, until the production bugs pile up or someone realizes a cron job could do the clipboard part cheaper. Take away their LLM tomorrow and they won’t suddenly start caring about ACH edge cases. They’ll just go back to shipping carelessness at a slower clip.
Look at Michael’s own example of ACH. The people keeping banking rails alive aren’t chiseling NACHA files into stone tablets to stay spiritually close to the metal. Their care shows up in reconciliation scripts, monitors, static checks, runbooks, and custom tooling they built because unaided human attention breaks down on systems this messy. Every jump up the abstraction ladder (compilers, garbage collectors, search engines, high-level frameworks) brought the exact same warning that we were moving another step away from the machine and losing the people who really understood it. Sure, far fewer programmers today can hand-assemble x86 than in 1985. Meanwhile, the systems we have to keep upright grew by several orders of magnitude. Without stronger leverage, you don’t get a golden age of artisanal engineering where everyone holds the whole codebase in their head. You just get more critical systems that nobody understands at all, because they long ago outgrew what one unaided brain can hold.
There is a bigger elephant in the room about all those outages, too, and it predates LLMs by a long shot. A huge share of the instability we are watching right now is the bill coming due for forty years of insufficient engineering rigor. Giving a shit does not make people infallible. Some of the smartest, most conscientious engineers in the industry spent decades building critical infrastructure in memory-unsafe languages, gluing together under-specified protocols, skipping formal verification, and shipping state machines whose edge cases lived only inside one person’s head. Heroics and tribal knowledge kept the wheels on, right up until they didn’t.
Plenty of the vulnerabilities and failure modes knocking systems over today have been sitting quietly in the wild for years, or even decades. We got away with them because nobody had the time or budget to poke every dark corner of a sprawling legacy stack, and because change moved slowly enough for manual patching to keep up. Only now is the issue being forced, by automated bug-hunting that never sleeps, by decades of accumulated coupling, and by systems that have finally grown too tangled for human heroics to paper over. Blaming all of that on AI slop is a comforting story, because it implies we can just go back to the old way of working and everything will steady out. The old way of working is how we ended up with a world where bad updates and long-dormant bugs can wobble major banks, airlines, and cloud providers in the same week.
None of that lets leadership off the hook. Where Michael is completely on target is what’s happening in the executive suite. Leadership looking at an LLM and thinking, fantastic, now we can lay off the prickly senior engineers who push back on bad ideas and replace them with a $200-a-month subscription, really is a slow-motion train wreck, and it makes a fragile landscape much worse. To someone who has never been paged at three in the morning, a fragile system held aloft by quiet competence and a pile of plausible-looking slop look identical on a quarterly slide deck.
That disease, though, is decades older than generative AI. It’s the exact same management fantasy that gave us “let’s fire the expensive in-house team and outsource the core platform to the lowest bidder,” “let’s cut QA because developers can test their own stuff,” and “let’s lay off twenty percent of engineering while keeping the roadmap unchanged.” AI didn’t invent the belief that engineers are interchangeable output factories. It just handed executives a shinier, cheaper-sounding excuse to run the same playbook again.
That’s why lumping AI-using engineers in with the executives hollowing out their companies does real harm. Telling the story as “AI makes engineers dumb and indifferent” accidentally writes bad leadership an alibi: shucks, the new technology didn’t live up to the hype, who could have known? And on the way there, it sneers at the people in the trenches who are grabbing every piece of leverage they can find to keep increasingly absurd systems from falling over.
If you want to know whether someone gives a shit about a system, asking whether they used an LLM is the wrong question. Ask what happens when the code they merged breaks at two in the morning. Ask whether “the model wrote it” flies as an excuse in code review. Ask whether they have the time, standing, and backing to tell a VP that a deadline is reckless.
Companies lose smart people who give a shit when they strip away ownership, punish dissent, and reward shipping volume over reliability. Give those same people real stakes and a good model, and they don’t check out. They finally get to build the guardrails, proofs, and fixes they never had the hours to build before.
Michael is right that capitalism has its hand squarely on a hot stove right now, and that the rest of us are getting burned while executives relearn that you can’t automate away accountability. I just wish we’d aim the anger at the people making that bet, instead of pretending that giving a shit requires typing every character by hand.
Cover: Jan Collaert I after Jan van der Straet (Stradanus), Nova Reperta: The Invention of Book Printing, c. 1600. CC0, source.

articles.title: Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy
articles.body:
Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy 67
			
		 	
				CNBC reports:
[Jensen Huang] told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.  A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present...
Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.   
The Independent notes that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's board Sunday "that he had more affairs beyond the two that were already in the public domain, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter."
Huang was reportedly "contrite" about his behavior during the crunch talks, and the board discussed "the importance of candor and honesty" with him, according to the newspaper.  
Elsewhere CNBC reports even President Trump's "staunchest allies" in the U.S. Congress "recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang..."
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States...."

articles.title: Nfs2root: A 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server
articles.body:
Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell.
Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd)
Fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Update the kernel and reboot.
What you need to know
- What: a pre-auth heap overflow in the kernel's NFS server, nfsd.
- Who: any Linux host serving NFSv4.1 or 4.2 (the default) on a reachable tcp/2049.
- Impact: one TCP connection writes 61 bytes past a kernel heap object; chained, that gives a root shell.
- Now: patch and reboot. Until then, firewall tcp/2049.
Key facts
- Severity 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N)
- Attack Remote, unauthenticated, tcp/2049
- Impact Kernel heap overflow → remote root shell
- Bug age 12 years, since Linux 3.16 (2014)
- Affected In-kernel nfsd with NFSv4.1 or 4.2
- Fixed in 6.12.117 · 6.18.61 · 7.3.2 · 7.4-rc1
One connection, no login
The NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes.
Twelve years in a few lines of C
Timeline
- Commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE. It ships in Linux 3.16.
- 12 yearsEvery kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels.
- Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report.
- OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own.
- CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes.
Watch it run
A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049.
Root cause
Each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how big that cache is.
Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.
That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.
The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.
From overflow to root
The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:
- Overflow The write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.
- Leak A replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.
- Free A forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.
- Reclaim We refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.
- Trigger We hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.
In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.
Found and proven by a machine
Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.
Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.
Am I exposed?
Tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.
Am I exposed?
What to do
Patch and reboot
On a distribution kernel, install the update that lists CVE-2026-99362.
Can't patch today? Close 2049
Or turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2
Then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.
Hunting for it
The attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:
- Kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, on every attempt, successful or not.
- Oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames.
- Shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server.
- Bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source.
Disclosure
We reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.
Credits
- OpenSec Intelligence: found the bug with Antara, which escalated it to pre-auth root on its own, and reported it with the full exploit and a patch.
- Jérémy Jean (ANSSI): found it independently and wrote the upstream fix, 5d5a72e965c8 and 241848cc774e.
- Chuck Lever and Jeff Layton: the NFSD maintainers.
References
nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slotThe upstream fix for CVE-2026-99362, by Jérémy Jean.github.com nfsd: set op->status when an operation's header cannot be encodedThe follow-up guard in the NFSv4 encoder.github.com
- Introduced by 47ee52986472 (Linux 3.16)
- Patch thread
- OpenSec's patch submission

The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.
That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.
The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.
From overflow to root
The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:
- Overflow The write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.
- Leak A replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.
- Free A forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.
- Reclaim We refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.
- Trigger We hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.
In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.
Found and proven by a machine
Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.
Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.
Am I exposed?
Tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.
Am I exposed?
What to do
Patch and reboot
On a distribution kernel, install the update that lists CVE-2026-99362.
Can't patch today? Close 2049
Or turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2
Then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.
Hunting for it
The attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:
- Kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, on every attempt, successful or not.
- Oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames.
- Shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server.
- Bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source.
Disclosure
We reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.
Credits
- OpenSec Intelligence: found the bug with Antara, which escalated it to pre-auth root on its own, and reported it with the full exploit and a patch.
- Jérémy Jean (ANSSI): found it independently and wrote the upstream fix, 5d5a72e965c8 and 241848cc774e.
- Chuck Lever and Jeff Layton: the NFSD maintainers.
References
nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slotThe upstream fix for CVE-2026-99362, by Jérémy Jean.github.com nfsd: set op->status when an operation's header cannot be encodedThe follow-up guard in the NFSv4 encoder.github.com
- Introduced by 47ee52986472 (Linux 3.16)
- Patch thread
- OpenSec's patch submission

articles.title: The year the web industry gave up
articles.body:
The year the web industry gave up
I’ve been drafting my personal “year in review” and one topic stood out as needing its own follow-up. So let’s get that out of the way!
Twenty twenty six, what an uneventful year, eh?
That’s sarcasm. The entire year has been nothing but incessant chatbot addicts toking their token pipes and shouting: “Everything has changed! Don’t get left behind!”
Despite regularly being mistaken for a software “engineer” I am but a humble website developer. And by “website developer” I mean website developer, not React developer; very different. Not that anyone understands this anymore. I’ll be lambasted for making fallacious “no true Scotsman” arguments for asserting that real web dev has actual standards.
Nevertheless, today I’m talking about/to the real web industry.
What’s left of it, anyway.
The web industry
TL;DR: the web industry is dismantling itself from the inside.
Events of the last year have been incomprehensibly stupid. The rapid deskilling and decimation of professional talent is a shock to the system. It’s demoralising to see once-respected peers drop all pretence of care for their profession.
Every week I sigh “et tu, Brute?” as I strike off another peer from my Christmas card list.
Web professionals are cashing in their credibility to shill for the AI industrial complex. People who have spent years, decades in some cases, building a reputation as leaders within the web industry are now destroying what they’ve built. They step on the heads of those who are fighting to stay afloat. I don’t need to name names, they won’t shut up about their chatbots. You know the type. They gush AI platitudes as if the singularity is holding a gun to their head. And they’ve solved everything! Web development? Chatbot. Web design? Chatbot. The websites they’re building? Believe it or not; chatbots.
And what has the web industry actually gained after all this performative slop?
- Entry level jobs have evaporated
- Web development education is in the gutter
- Web infrastructure is getting hammered
It’s embarrassing how much the web industry has lost in so little time. It has cannibalised itself and those responsible seem oblivious to the cause and effect of their actions.
Let’s get one thing absolutely clear: there is no career in prompting. There is no scenario where replacing your work with a chatbot will have a long-term positive impact on your career. Unless you’re into S&M at the beck and call of billionaires. I mean, I don’t want to kink shame, but keep it out off the workplace, please!
The “it’s just a tool” and “inevitable” rhetoric doesn’t cut it. For heaven’s sake, even if you continue to ignore all other moral an ethical issues, at least open your eyes to the absurdity of what’s being sold here. Tokens are not the commodity, you are.
Replacing professionally trained skills with markdown files and ceding control to chatbot subscriptions is not a sustainable future for the web industry. I’m not here to debate whether chatbot-driven web design/development is “good enough”. Although I’ll note that many who claim this are confusing “taste” with the trained talent they’ve driven out of town.
What possible positive future are we expecting by locking knowledge and workflow behind a chatbot subscription? How is this even a question that needs asking?
To be honest, it’s hard to blame those who’ve decided to give up and ride chatbots all the way down. It’s certainly easier than remaining optimistic about the web industry in face of the grifters who dominate the conversation. You must know one thing though: the AI boosters in our industry are a vocal minority. Those suffering to maintain sanity are silenced by AI mandates and fear of repercussions. Not me though. I’m in a position to call out this bullshit. I do so because every week I get heartbreaking emails and private DMs from those suffering. That’s why I write what I write. People are hurting. You’re not alone people!
I encourage everyone to look outside the bubble and realise that the rest of humanity thinks “AI” is the dumbest shit the tech industry has ever shat.
Do not allow your brain to atrophy just because “everyone else is doing it.”
If you’ve lost respect for the web, if you’re destroying the web on behalf of gatekeepers like Google — there’s a topic for another post — do the rest of us a favour and leave. If you haven’t given up, tell people. We need more voices speaking up against this nonsense.
I’m not giving up. I’ll continue to fight for a human web.
