articles.title: 1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe
articles.body:
1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe (techcrunch.com) 10
			
		 	
				Password manager 1Password has confirmed that hackers breached its internal systems on November 19 after gaining access to an employee's corporate GitHub account and pushing malicious code to company servers. The attacker stole customer names, email addresses, account creation dates and last login timestamps, but 1Password said customer password vaults were "at no point" accessible to the attacker and that its apps and browser extensions remain unaffected. TechCrunch reports:  It's unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee's corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch's questions about the incident. 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. [...] The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

articles.title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You'll Be the Main Character.
articles.body:
Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You'll Be the Main Character. (404media.co) 67
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader schwit1 shares a report from 404 Media: Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized "shows" starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.
Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don't end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called "creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user," describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called "My Channel," which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make "the user as the protagonist for the whole video." The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.
"You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist," a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. "The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the  of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the  of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The  and  parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred."

articles.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
articles.body:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann
Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the
axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.
- grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md.
- grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.
Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.
Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).
The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.
Apache 2.0, Copyright 2026 Anthropic, PBC. See LICENSE, and NOTICE and
ATTRIBUTION.md in each folder.

articles.title: Britain's ghost stations
articles.body:
When I stepped off a train at Achanalt station into the frosty Highlands one morning last March, I did notice that it wasn’t quite Waterloo in the rush hour, but I didn’t realise what an exclusive club I had just joined. According to a list of Britain’s most and least-used stations published this week, I was one of only 352 people to board or get off a train there in the entire 12 months from April 2025 to March 2026.
Flanders and Swann wrote ‘The Slow Train’ about the Beeching closures, lamenting the rural stations which were to close. They needn’t have worried: over half a century on, such places still exist.
My instinct is to attack the waste of public money in keeping a station open when hardly anyone uses it, but the absurdity of Britain’s ‘ghost’ stations fascinates me more than angers me. In any case, having paid £11 to travel 20 miles down the line from Strathcarron, I did rather feel that I had single-handedly covered the annual cost of maintaining what is really little more than a platform and Perspex shelter.
Achanalt, it turns out, is only the 15th least-used station in Britain. The honour of being the least-used this year is taken by Reddish South, on an obscure line from Stockport to Stalybridge in Greater Manchester, which was used by only 94 passengers. It is an achievement it will be hard-pressed to repeat next year, as the country’s least-used station invariably receives a leap in custom as railway fanatics descend on it just for the sake of being there: station-visiting has apparently taken over from train-spotting now that few trains have proper locomotives any more. Last year’s winner of the title for least-used station, Elton and Orston, in Nottinghamshire, saw its annual passenger numbers jump from 68 to 102, demoting it to third place. I wouldn’t be surprised if every single one of the extra passengers wore an anorak and carried a bag of Marmite sandwiches.
There are two types of ghost station. Firstly, there are those such as Reddish South which are the product of public opposition to the Beeching closures. Some time in the 1970s, British Rail stopped closing stations, reckoning that the bureaucracy and expense of going through the consultation procedure required to remove them from the railway map altogether was greater than simply running down the service to a minimal level. As a result, Reddish South receives one train a week in each direction, on a Saturday morning. You can’t even get a day out in Stockport: catch the 8.46 from Reddish South and you only get five minutes before the train home.
The second type of ghost station is those like Achanalt, which offer a full service of several trains a day; it is just that there aren’t many people who want to travel there. In Achanalt’s case, it isn’t hard to wonder why. The ‘village’, if it can be called that, consists of four houses. Nor is the station all that much good for doing what I was doing: accessing the nearby hills, as a river cuts them off to the south and a thick forestry plantation lies in the way to the north. If you want to go for a walk, it is almost certainly going to involve a few miles’ romp along the A832.
It is pretty absurd that Dr Beeching left a station like this open while depriving Dudley (population 335,000) and Mansfield (114,000) of a rail service – although the latter has subsequently reopened. But at least Achanalt serves four properties. Even more bizarre is Altnabreac station on the Far North Line between Inverness and Wick.
Maybe Dr Beeching couldn’t even find it on the map. It lies up a track seven miles from the nearest public road and there is precisely one house within five miles: the former station house. Trouble is, owners, who presumably could have bought a remote property anywhere in the empty vastness of Caithness, don’t seem to like trains very much. In 2023, a gang of workers from Network Rail turned up to repair the platform and found the gate locked. After a stand-off lasting many months, involving many lawyers and a court case, and a threat by Network Rail to compulsorily purchase the property so that access could be restored, an injunction finally gave the work gang access.
In the meantime, no trains ran at all: the official passenger numbers for the year 2024/25 were zero. Happily, services have now been restored and the walkers and bird-spotters have returned to the platform. Er, all 172 of them last year.

articles.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
articles.body:
Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release (axios.com) 60
			
		 	
				Axios reports:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates...
The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. 
Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.  This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. 
There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

articles.title: Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe
articles.body:
Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe (arstechnica.com) 116
			
		 	
				The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has opened an investigation into an Amazon Prime Air delivery drone that struck a fiber-optic cable and crashed onto a residential garage in Michigan after delivering shampoo. The drone lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines, prompting Amazon and local utility workers to coordinate its removal. Amazon offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card. Ars Technica reports:  Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case -- so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as "UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." That notice was posted on November 23. The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents. 
Amazon said the Michigan crash was the first involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit, but federal regulators are already investigating several incidents in Arizona and Texas involving collisions with a construction crane, an internet cable, and an apartment building.
An Amazon spokesperson said Prime Air drones make nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered "hundreds of thousands of packages this year."

articles.title: Deriving Black-Scholes
articles.body:
Deriving Black-Scholes
Option price from the no-arbitrage hypothesis.
Even if it feels unintuitive, the price of an option does not depend on whether you expect the underlying to moon or tank. Under some reasonable market hypotheses, we can build a fully hedged portfolio by holding the underlying and shorting the option. Since it is riskless, by no-arbitrage assumption, it must return the same as the risk-free interest rate. That allows to put together an equation (the Black-Scholes equation), and solve for the option price (the Black-Scholes formula).
Model §
A European call gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying at a fixed price \(K\!\), the strike, on a fixed date \(T\!\), the maturity. Its value \(V\!\) is the premium you need to pay for having that optionality, and it depends on time and on the underlying stock price \(S\!\). At maturity it is the payoff1 1 For example, pay $5 today for the right to buy one AMZN share for $200 in a month. If AMZN then trades at $230, you buy at $200 and the option is worth $30. If it trades at $180, you walk away and the option is worth nothing.
\[V(T,S)=\max(S-K,0).\]
Stock moves scale with price, so it is common to model the returns instead of the price. Over a short time the return is a small drift plus noise. The noise is the sum of many small, unpredictable2 2 Weak-form efficient market hypothesis: past prices do not predict future moves. sources. Such sum can be modeled as a Brownian motion \(W\!\),3 3 By the central limit theorem, the sum of many small independent variables is normal. so the return is
\[\frac{dS}{S}=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW\!,\]
with drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma\!\). For our model, we will assume constant drift, volatility and interest rate \(r\!\). We will also assume “perfect” trading, with fractional shares allowed, no fees, no taxes, no dividends, and no arbitrage.
Hedged portfolio §
The trick of Black-Scholes is to build a fully hedged portfolio combining the option and the underlying in the right proportion. By the no-arbitrage hypothesis, its returns must be the same as the interest rate \(r\!\), and that way we can put together an equation.
When the stock moves a little, the option moves by \(\Delta\) times as much, with
\[\Delta=\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}.\]
If you short one option and hold \(\Delta\) shares, then the two moves cancel. This is a delta hedge.
Note that \(\Delta\) changes with the stock price and time. The portfolio is riskless only over an instant, and stays so only if it is rebalanced continuously.
Black-Scholes equation §
Use the Taylor expansion of the option value and keep the terms up to order \(dt\). Since \((dW)^2=dt\), the \((dS)^2\) term is one of them,
\[dV=\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}dt+\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}dS +\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}(dS)^2.\]
Substituting the stock model gives
\[dV=\left(\mu S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt +\sigma S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\,dW.\]
Now, we can use the same hedged portfolio \(\Pi\) as before, short one option and long \(\Delta\) shares, which is worth \(-V+\Delta S\!\). Holding \(\Delta\) fixed over an instant,
\[d\Pi=-dV+\Delta dS,\]
and substituting \(dS\) and \(dV\!\) gives
\[d\Pi=\left(-\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} -\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt.\]
See how noise and drift cancel. No \(dW\!\) term is left, and everything else is known at time \(t\), so over the next instant the portfolio change is fixed.4 4 A known return with no randomness is precisely what riskless means. We’ve built a riskless portfolio, that by the no-arbitrage assumption, it must earn the risk-free rate, \(d\Pi=r\Pi\,dt.\) Equating both expressions gives us the Black-Scholes equation
\[\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}+rS\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}=rV.\]
Note that \(\mu\) is gone, so the option price does not depend on the drift.
Black-Scholes formula §
I won’t bore you with the technical details,5 5 For the details, see John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 11th edition, Pearson, 2021. The Bible of derivatives. but the above equation can be solved by a change of variables to turn it into the heat equation, whose solution is known. Define
\[\tau=T-t,\quad x=\ln S+\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau,\quad V(t,S)=e^{-r\tau}w(\tau,x),\]
where \(w\) is the option value at maturity. Substituting, all terms but two cancel, and we get the heat equation
\[\frac{\partial w}{\partial\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial x^2}.\]
With the payoff as initial condition, the solution is
\[w(\tau,x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2\tau}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \max(e^y-K,0)\,\exp\left(-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2\tau}\right)dy.\]
Completing the squares gives the Black-Scholes formula
\[V(t,S)=S\,N(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2),\]
where \(N\) is the standard normal CDF and
\[d_1=\frac{\ln(S/K)+\left(r+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{\tau}.\]
- \(N(d_1)\) is the hedge ratio \(\Delta\), so the first term represents the price of an asset-or-nothing call, which pays the share if the call ends in the money.
- \(N(d_2)\) is the risk-neutral probability of exercise, so the second term is the present value of the expected strike payment.
That’s all, lads, go make Ken Griffin broke.

articles.title: Swift Death of Statelessness
articles.body:
Swift Death of Statelessness
My drive home from work is always spent in total silence. The monotony of Route 101 (it's not a flex) has an uncanny way of clearing cognitive noise. Today, somewhere in that quiet stretch of highway, reflecting on my work in the Kubernetes ecosystem, it struck me just how completely our industry is reinventing itself.
For 15 years, cloud computing was worshiping a statelessness as an absolute deity. Build stateless containers, spin them up dynamically, let them die without consequence. And this architecture was simple, resilient, and economically predictable.
And then AI happened, violently dismantling prior art. Reasoning models and multi-turn agentic workflows are inherently stateful. Every interaction carries a prompt history, a context window, and an expensive KV-cache. When you route a prompt to an arbitrary node using standard round-robin load balancing, you discard that cache. You force saturated GPUs to recompute tokens that were already processed milliseconds ago.
In economics, we call this pure deadweight loss. In distributed systems, it's referred as cache thrashing. The architectural frontier of networking is no longer about blindly moving packets from point A to point B. It is an economic allocation problem: balancing network transport latency against the marginal cost of GPU recomputation.
We spent a decade decoupling state from compute. Now the laws of physics and economics are forcing us to design intelligent proxies to put them back in the same room.

articles.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
articles.body:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.
FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.
The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.
SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.
Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments)
Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments)
I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.
p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

articles.title: Spending 35B Opus 5.5 Tokens to Write a Symphony
articles.body:
Back to blog
Opus 5.5 writes its Magnum Opus (2500 times)
A four-movement symphony for full orchestra. Claude wrote it, recorded it and made the video, over about 2,500 rounds of review.
  "I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude"
So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition. Basically, I did the meme:
You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:
YouTube picks the picture quality from your connection and the size of the player. For a sharper score, choose 1080p or higher under the gear icon, or go full screen.
- 4movements
- 929bars
- 22,979notes
- 25 minof music
- 35BOpus tokens, roughly
The full scores, as PDF:
The source of the scores, the critics' reviews and the scripts are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
These are virtual instruments, so the audio quality is not as good as if an orchestra recorded this live. But its pretty good, and considering Claude did all of the mockup and rendering in a DAW with pro-level VSTs, I'd say the result is still pretty impressive.
The whole thing used around 35 billion Opus tokens.
We used Claude Code Projects (beta) for this, and I find it really useful for project-based coding. The orchestrator / thread model worked really well for us in practice. Generally, each movement was owned by a thread.
I thought the process I used to achieve this was pretty interesting, so I decided to write it up.
tl;dr - For things that can't be 'verified' as good or bad like art/music, just make the agent do more iterations, way more iterations than you think.
There were three jobs: writing the symphony, turning the score into a recording, and making the video. I'll go through them in that order.
Part 1: Writing the symphony
Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.
The music is written as text
  Claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number: c4 is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.
Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.
The first theme of Movement I, as Claude typed it
These eight bars for the first violins are copied from the score's source text. Point at a note in the text or on the staff to find it in the other. Click a note to hear it.
Swipe the staff sideways to see all of it.
"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.
One Claude writes, another reviews
The method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.
- The composer writes a version of a movement.
- A new critic, which has never seen the piece before, studies it and suggests specific fixes.
- The composer decides which fixes to accept.
- The result becomes the next version, and a new critic starts again.
Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.
Each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.
Originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.
Every round, from the written log
Each square is one round. Time runs from left to right, ten rounds per column, and each of the ten rows is one critic's subject. Pick a square to read that round's line in the log.
Swipe the grid sideways to see later rounds.
Loading the log…
    the log records a change
    the log says nothing was changed
These are the real lines from the log, cut to about 200 characters. They are written in the working shorthand of the loop, with bar numbers and instrument names.
  
Critics had to read the textbooks
A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.
One example: an orchestration textbook says that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.
Great symphonies as models
Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?
What I did
I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.
I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.
Version 1 next to the final version
I thought it would be neat to compare version 1 of each movement against the final version. There are no high quality recordings of version 1, so both are played here with the same basic MIDI sounds, which is the closest thing to compare.
Version 1 against the final version
The strip is the final version of the movement, one segment per bar. The brighter a bar, the more of its notes are new or changed since version 1. Click anywhere on the strip to play from that bar, and switch between the two versions while it plays.
A note counts as kept when version 1 has the same pitch at the same place in the matching bar. A pitch played by several instruments at once counts once. A program matched the bars of the two versions, so the shading is approximate. Both versions are set to the same volume.
Version 1 of Movement I was a sketch for strings only, and its first theme was different. In Movements II, III and IV the main themes begin with the same notes in version 1 and in the final version, and the bright bars on the strips show where the changes are. By the count described above, about 14% of the notes in the final Movement I were already in version 1, 35% in Movement II, 61% in Movement III and 55% in Movement IV.
What to keep in mind
Claude wrote 99.9% of every single element of the composition. I maybe influenced a measure or two of note selection over the whole process.
Part 2: Turning the score into a recording
A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.
The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.
The tools
Two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.)
Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.
Claude cannot hear
A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:
- Is the melody louder than the accompaniment?
- Does each note start on the beat?
- When a loud chord stops, does the sound die away as fast as it does on a real orchestra recording?
The loop
Each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:
- Record the movement.
- Three critics measure the recording. Each critic is a separate Claude with one job. One checks how the notes are played. One checks the balance between instruments. One checks something different each round, such as the timing or the sound of the room.
- Each critic writes a short list of the worst problems, with evidence and a suggested fix.
- Another Claude decides which fixes to make, changes the scripts and records again.
The four movements took 184 rounds in total.
The opening of the finale at six stages
The same 18 bars, from the basic computer playback to the final recording. Pick a stage to hear it. You can switch while it plays.
All six clips are set to the same volume here, so the differences you hear are in the playing and the mix. As first made, rounds 0 to 11 were 5 to 6 dB quieter than rounds 20 and 30.
My listening
The measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.
Each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:
- Too wet. The reverb was cut in half and shortened.
- A volume change on almost every note. I opened a project and saw that the loop had been fixing problems by moving the volume fader note by note. No person works that way. All of those moves were removed, and the problems were fixed the way a person would fix them: by changing how the instrument plays the note.
Learning from people who do this by hand
About a month in, we studied how professionals make mockups. The sources were YouTube tutorials by film-score mixers, the sample library maker's own template project, and project files that composers have shared for others to study. Three lessons changed the recordings most: use less reverb, shape each phrase so it rises and falls, and leave a small gap between repeated notes.
Part 3: Making the video
The last job was the video at the YouTube link above.
Each video shows the orchestra's sheet music as a dark page. Every note lights up at the moment it sounds, in a color for its instrument, and a small light hops from note to note along each instrument's line. A program worked all of this out from the written score and the recording.
Finding the notes
Like I said above, the score is written as text in LilyPond. For the videos, LilyPond printed each movement as one long line and also wrote down where on the page it put every note. That gave the video program the exact place of all 22,979 notes.
Staying in time
The recording speeds up and slows down, as any performance does. REAPER, the software that made the recording, keeps a list of every change of speed. The video program uses that list to work out the second at which each note sounds. The lights land within two hundredths of a second of the sound.
Pointing the camera
An orchestra's score is too tall to fit on the screen, so the camera shows only part of the page. It goes to the instruments that are loudest in the recording at that moment. The program plans the camera's whole route before it draws anything, so the camera moves seldom and arrives before the passage it is moving to begins. When two instruments far apart on the page matter at the same time, the screen splits in two.
Words on the page
Each instrument's name is printed on the page where it starts to play. Short labels, 124 in all, point out what a music theory class would: a theme coming back, an unusual chord, a quotation from an earlier movement. One Claude wrote the labels from the score, and a second Claude checked every one against the notes.
Watching and fixing
I watched each version and said what looked wrong. The camera jerked around. The instrument names shifted about. The opening took 19 seconds to reach the first sound. Each comment led to a fix, and the videos were made five times in two days. The four movements were then joined into one 25-minute video for YouTube, and its music now starts in the first second.
Adding it up
So that's the whole process. Add it up and it's about 2,400 rounds on the score, 184 on the recordings and 5 on the video. That's roughly the 2500 in the title.
None of those rounds had a pass/fail test, because there isn't one for whether music is good. What I could do was give each critic one narrow thing to check, make it back up its opinion with a textbook or a measurement, and run the loop way more times than seemed necessary. Then I listened to the result myself, because Claude can't.
Credits
- Composer: Opus 5.5
- Assistant for the final mockup recordings and the video: Fable
- Human overseer: Dan Price (me)
GitHub repo
The scores, the reviews and the scripts from this project are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
For orchestras
If you are with a professional symphony orchestra and might be interested in performing this live, please reach out to me. I'm on X at x.com/gooby_esq, or you can email me at [email protected].

articles.title: Spending 35B Opus 5.5 Tokens to Write a Symphony
articles.body:
Back to blog
Opus 5.5 writes its Magnum Opus (2500 times)
A four-movement symphony for full orchestra. Claude wrote it, recorded it and made the video, over about 2,500 rounds of review.
  "I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude"
So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition. Basically, I did the meme:
You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:
YouTube picks the picture quality from your connection and the size of the player. For a sharper score, choose 1080p or higher under the gear icon, or go full screen.
- 4movements
- 929bars
- 22,979notes
- 25 minof music
- 35BOpus tokens, roughly
The full scores, as PDF:
The source of the scores, the critics' reviews and the scripts are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony
These are virtual instruments, so the audio quality is not as good as if an orchestra recorded this live. But its pretty good, and considering Claude did all of the mockup and rendering in a DAW with pro-level VSTs, I'd say the result is still pretty impressive.
The whole thing used around 35 billion Opus tokens.
We used Claude Code Projects (beta) for this, and I find it really useful for project-based coding. The orchestrator / thread model worked really well for us in practice. Generally, each movement was owned by a thread.
I thought the process I used to achieve this was pretty interesting, so I decided to write it up.
tl;dr - For things that can't be 'verified' as good or bad like art/music, just make the agent do more iterations, way more iterations than you think.
There were three jobs: writing the symphony, turning the score into a recording, and making the video. I'll go through them in that order.
Part 1: Writing the symphony
Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.
The music is written as text
  Claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number: c4 is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.
Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.
The first theme of Movement I, as Claude typed it
These eight bars for the first violins are copied from the score's source text. Point at a note in the text or on the staff to find it in the other. Click a note to hear it.
Swipe the staff sideways to see all of it.
"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.
One Claude writes, another reviews
The method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.
- The composer writes a version of a movement.
- A new critic, which has never seen the piece before, studies it and suggests specific fixes.
- The composer decides which fixes to accept.
- The result becomes the next version, and a new critic starts again.
Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.
Each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.
Originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.
Every round, from the written log
Each square is one round. Time runs from left to right, ten rounds per column, and each of the ten rows is one critic's subject. Pick a square to read that round's line in the log.
Swipe the grid sideways to see later rounds.
Loading the log…
    the log records a change
    the log says nothing was changed
These are the real lines from the log, cut to about 200 characters. They are written in the working shorthand of the loop, with bar numbers and instrument names.
  
Critics had to read the textbooks
A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.
One example: an orchestration textbook says that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.
Great symphonies as models
Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?
What I did
I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.
I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.
Version 1 next to the final version
I thought it would be neat to compare version 1 of each movement against the final version. There are no high quality recordings of version 1, so both are played here with the same basic MIDI sounds, which is the closest thing to compare.
Version 1 against the final version
The strip is the final version of the movement, one segment per bar. The brighter a bar, the more of its notes are new or changed since version 1. Click anywhere on the strip to play from that bar, and switch between the two versions while it plays.
A note counts as kept when version 1 has the same pitch at the same place in the matching bar. A pitch played by several instruments at once counts once. A program matched the bars of the two versions, so the shading is approximate. Both versions are set to the same volume.
Version 1 of Movement I was a sketch for strings only, and its first theme was different. In Movements II, III and IV the main themes begin with the same notes in version 1 and in the final version, and the bright bars on the strips show where the changes are. By the count described above, about 14% of the notes in the final Movement I were already in version 1, 35% in Movement II, 61% in Movement III and 55% in Movement IV.
What to keep in mind
Claude wrote 99.9% of every single element of the composition. I maybe influenced a measure or two of note selection over the whole process.
Part 2: Turning the score into a recording
A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.
The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.
The tools
Two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.)
Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.
Claude cannot hear
A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:
- Is the melody louder than the accompaniment?
- Does each note start on the beat?
- When a loud chord stops, does the sound die away as fast as it does on a real orchestra recording?
The loop
Each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:
- Record the movement.
- Three critics measure the recording. Each critic is a separate Claude with one job. One checks how the notes are played. One checks the balance between instruments. One checks something different each round, such as the timing or the sound of the room.
- Each critic writes a short list of the worst problems, with evidence and a suggested fix.
- Another Claude decides which fixes to make, changes the scripts and records again.
The four movements took 184 rounds in total.
The opening of the finale at six stages
The same 18 bars, from the basic computer playback to the final recording. Pick a stage to hear it. You can switch while it plays.
All six clips are set to the same volume here, so the differences you hear are in the playing and the mix. As first made, rounds 0 to 11 were 5 to 6 dB quieter than rounds 20 and 30.
My listening
The measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.
Each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:

articles.title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
articles.body:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.
Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.
Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”
As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.
The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

articles.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs
articles.body:
I checked Clojure's core with Lean and differential testing and found unreported bugs in HAMT and vector-of
I read Koukyosyumei's article "著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.
Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.
hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.
I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples.
I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.
I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org.
They include reduce on vector-of, the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.
The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries.
The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.
I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21. The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.
How I checked
The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.
You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.
If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations.
So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of %.
When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.
Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results.
For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.
For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.
The operations were conj, pop, assoc, and their transient versions.
I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.
reduce on vector-of never finishes
vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.
Clojure implements it in gvec.clj, written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector.
If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65504))))
;; => 2145354256
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65505))))
;; => never returns
(reduce + (drop 1 (vec (range 65505))))
;; => 2145419760
The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj, where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.
(recur result (bit-and 0xffe0 (+ aidx 32)))
The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.
With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.
After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.
The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce.
In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32.
import Std.Tactic.BVDecide
def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32)
def stepFix (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := (~~~0x1f) &&& (a + 32)
theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepImpl a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepImpl; bv_decide
theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepFix a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepFix; bv_decide
impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792, and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well.
fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0.
dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key
Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree.
Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with =.
HashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed.
It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash, but it passes the parameter hash instead.
return new HashCollisionNode(null, hash, count - 1, removePair(array, idx/2));
The parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc.
If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.
In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently.
CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.
In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.
(def a (java.util.ArrayList. [0 42]))
(def b (java.util.ArrayList. [1 11]))
[(hash a) (hash b) (hash [0 42]) (= a [0 42])]
;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true]
(def m3 (-> (hash-map a :A b :B)
            (dissoc [0 42])
            (assoc a :A2)))
[m3 (count m3) (get m3 b)]
;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]
When you print m3, you can see the key b, but (get m3 b) returns nil.
After the dissoc, the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42].
The next assoc then concludes that a, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.
A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b.
In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.
disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.
I changed that line in the 1.12.7 PersistentHashMap.java to this.hash and compiled it.
With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned :B for (get m3 b).
removeIf gives different results with and without a type hint
Since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface. CLJ-2864 removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.
In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.
The compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type.
A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn.
That method still applies RT.booleanCast to a boolean return value, so the same .removeIf call gives a different result depending on the type hint.
(let [l (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3])]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => ClassCastException
(let [l (identity (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3]))]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => [3]
Wrapping the list in identity hides the type of l, so the call goes through reflection.
A set used as a function returns the element itself.
In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the Long into a Boolean and throws.
The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.
int overflow and a negative subvec index
Clojure 1.12 added IDrop implementations that make drop faster.
The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and n as ints and then compare the sum with the length.
StringSeq.drop for string seqs is one of them.
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (next (seq "abc")))
;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (seq "abc"))
;; => ()
The Lean model gave the counterexample i = 2147483646 and n = 2147483647.
I changed the check to compare n with the remaining length s.length() - i.
Under the assumptions 0 < i < s.length()= and 0 < n, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.
For assoc on the result of subvec, SubVector.assocN does not reject a negative index.
(assoc [2 3] -1 :x)
;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException
(let [s (assoc (subvec [0 1 2 3 4] 2 4) -1 :x)]
  [s (.-v s)])
;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]
The call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged.
CLJ-962 fixed the same bug in nth, but assoc still has it.
Other findings
The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.
Where I found nothing
PersistentHashMap and PersistentHashSet matched java.util.HashMap over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates.
The tests also covered maps before an update staying unchanged, ArrayNode splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.
PersistentTreeMap matched java.util.TreeMap and kept the red-black tree invariants.
Vectors matched ArrayList around every tree boundary I tested.
On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check Numbers uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.
For multiplication, bv_decide timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits.
I proved up to 32 bits that clojure.core/mod matches the floored remainder.
Every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article. I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.
You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.
If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations.
So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of %.
When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.
Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results.
For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.
For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.
The operations were conj, pop, assoc, and their transient versions.
I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.
reduce on vector-of never finishes
vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.
Clojure implements it in gvec.clj, written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector.
If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65504))))
;; => 2145354256
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65505))))
;; => never returns
(reduce + (drop 1 (vec (range 65505))))
;; => 2145419760
The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj, where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.
(recur result (bit-and 0xffe0 (+ aidx 32)))
The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.
With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.
After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.
The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce.
In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32.
import Std.Tactic.BVDecide
def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32)
def stepFix (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := (~~~0x1f) &&& (a + 32)
theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepImpl a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepImpl; bv_decide
theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepFix a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepFix; bv_decide
impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792, and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well.
fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0.
dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key
Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree.
Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with =.
HashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed.
It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash, but it passes the parameter hash instead.
return new HashCollisionNode(null, hash, count - 1, removePair(array, idx/2));
The parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc.
If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.
In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently.
CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.
In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.
(def a (java.util.ArrayList. [0 42]))
(def b (java.util.ArrayList. [1 11]))
[(hash a) (hash b) (hash [0 42]) (= a [0 42])]
;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true]
(def m3 (-> (hash-map a :A b :B)
            (dissoc [0 42])
            (assoc a :A2)))
[m3 (count m3) (get m3 b)]
;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]
When you print m3, you can see the key b, but (get m3 b) returns nil.
After the dissoc, the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42].
The next assoc then concludes that a, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.
A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b.
In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.
disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.
I changed that line in the 1.12.7 PersistentHashMap.java to this.hash and compiled it.
With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned :B for (get m3 b).
removeIf gives different results with and without a type hint
Since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface. CLJ-2864 removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.
In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.
The compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type.
A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn.
That method still applies RT.booleanCast to a boolean return value, so the same .removeIf call gives a different result depending on the type hint.
(let [l (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3])]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => ClassCastException
(let [l (identity (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3]))]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => [3]
Wrapping the list in identity hides the type of l, so the call goes through reflection.
A set used as a function returns the element itself.
In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the Long into a Boolean and throws.
The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.
int overflow and a negative subvec index
Clojure 1.12 added IDrop implementations that make drop faster.
The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and n as ints and then compare the sum with the length.
StringSeq.drop for string seqs is one of them.
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (next (seq "abc")))
;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (seq "abc"))
;; => ()
The Lean model gave the counterexample i = 2147483646 and n = 2147483647.
I changed the check to compare n with the remaining length s.length() - i.
Under the assumptions 0 < i < s.length()= and 0 < n, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.
For assoc on the result of subvec, SubVector.assocN does not reject a negative index.
(assoc [2 3] -1 :x)
;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException
(let [s (assoc (subvec [0 1 2 3 4] 2 4) -1 :x)]
  [s (.-v s)])
;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]
The call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged.
CLJ-962 fixed the same bug in nth, but assoc still has it.
Other findings
The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.
Where I found nothing
PersistentHashMap and PersistentHashSet matched java.util.HashMap over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates.
The tests also covered maps before an update staying unchanged, ArrayNode splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.
PersistentTreeMap matched java.util.TreeMap and kept the red-black tree invariants.
Vectors matched ArrayList around every tree boundary I tested.
On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check Numbers uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.
For multiplication, bv_decide timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits.
I proved up to 32 bits that clojure.core/mod matches the floored remainder.
Every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article. I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

All-Clad’s Black Friday Sale Just Started, and These 7 Deals Can Save You Up to 48%
Looking for more great deals? Browse our master list of current sales (updated daily!) and check out our Black Friday & Cyber Monday hub for all our latest coverage.
All-Clad is a chef-loved cookware brand that is known for its quality stainless steel pots and pans. Our shopping writer also absolutely adores the nonstick line (she uses it every day!). So if you’re in the market for time-tested pots and pans, then you’re in luck: All-Clad’s Black Friday sale is here!
Right now you can save hundreds on cookware sets, and snag individual pots and pans for way less too. We found seven can’t-miss deals from All-Clad’s Black Friday sale, so you can save big with little effort. Happy shopping!
1. D3 Everyday Stainless 12.5-Inch Skillet with Lid
Save yourself 50 bucks when you pick up this roomy stainless steel pan (and lid!) from All-Clad for just $120. It’s oven-safe up to 600°F and compatible with all stovetops. Prepare to use this pan, well, every day.
2. NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick Fry Pan Set
Score this set of three nonstick pans for $110 off right now. You’ll get 8-, 10-, and 12-inch pans, all with a slick, ceramic nonstick coating. “I’m genuinely so impressed by how nonstick these pans actually are,” Shopping Writer Micki Wagner writes in her NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick Fry Pan Set review. “They have quickly become my favorite nonstick pans. I actually look forward to using them.”
3. D3 Everyday Stainless 10-Piece Set
Looking to completely upgrade your cookware? Grab this 10-piece set that includes a 3-quart lidded sauté pan, two skillets (an 8.5-inch and a 10.5-inch), a 6-quart lidded stockpot, and two lidded saucepans (a 1.5-quart and a 3-quart). Not only does this set have most everything you need, but it’s also on sale for nearly $400 off this Black Friday.
4. D3 Everyday Stainless 3-Piece Sauce Pan & Potato Masher Set with Lid
Now that we are firmly in the holiday season, mashed potatoes are a must. With this set, you’ll have the cookware you need to make this beloved side. This set features a lidded 3-quart saucepan and a potato masher — so if you can’t find yours in your junk drawer, no worries. Plus it’s 48% off right now, so you can get it for just $130.
5. NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick 6-Quart Sauté Pan with Lid
A good sauté pan is a piece of cookware you might find yourself using all throughout the week. It’s perfect for browning ground beef, searing steaks, pan-frying chicken cutlets, and making one-skillet meals. This lidded 6-quart nonstick version from All-Clad has a 5-star rating and is currently on sale for $180. Run, don’t walk, to take advantage of this deal.
6. D3 Stainless 5-Quart Casserole with Lid
’Tis the season for large gatherings and meals that feed a crowd. This 5-quart casserole pan is nice and roomy, without being as deep as a stockpot, so it’s great for baked pastas, soups and stews, fruit cobblers, and more. Plus, it’s currently on sale for $150. If you’re hosting or in charge of bringing a casserole, pick up this highly rated pan while it’s discounted.
7. NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP: Very Iconic Pan
This versatile new pan from All-Clad is already on sale this Black Friday! And if you’re looking for a do-it-all pan, seriously look no further. This this 7-in-1 (6-quart) pan comes with a glass lid, a steamer insert, and a roasting rack, so you can make pasta, boil potatoes, brown ground beef, roast pork tenderloin, and so much more. Plus, it can go from your stove to an oven as hot as 450°F for maximum versatility.
Why You Should Trust Me
I’ve been a journalist for nearly a decade and have tested hundreds of products for the kitchen, home, and beyond since 2022. I only write about the cookware, appliances, and ingredients that truly impress me or come highly recommended from trusted experts. The recommendations above aren’t paid endorsements; they are editorially vetted products from our team.
